source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Turner

verdict.trueWording: Asymmetrical stylistic arch

Lee: 'Alan Turner (2014) proposed four areas one could explore to get to the bottom of what is good (or perceived as bad) style in The Lord of the Rings: - The linguistic registers given to different characters - Asymmetrical stylistic arch - Semantic archaisms - Syntactic archaisms'. All four areas match the claim in the same order.

claim: Lee reports that Drout's 2004 Tolkien Studies article observed repetition, mirroring and non-standard sentence structure as deliberate stylistic effects.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF), citing Drout 2004

verdict.trueWording: repetition and mirroring, and non-standard sentence structure
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'For example, Drout (2004) observed repetition and mirroring, and non-standard sentence structure.' The journal attribution also checks out against Lee's bibliography: 'Drout, Michael D.C. 2004. "Tolkien's Prose Style and its Literary and Rhetorical Effects." Tolkien Studies 1, 137-163.' Lee frames these as 'common devices used by Tolkien', supporting the claim's 'deliberate stylistic effects'.

claim: Drout and Wynne judge the biggest failing of Tolkien criticism to be its lack of discussion of sentence-level writing, word choice and syntax, crediting Shippey, Rosebury, Flieger and Thomas as exceptions.
source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), via ORA
quote: his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax

verdict.trueWording: his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'The biggest failing in Tolkien criticism, however, is its lack of discussion of Tolkien's style, his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax.' (Extraction shows 'choiceand' — a PDF line-break artifact, not a wording difference.) All four exceptions confirmed: 'Shippey's Road and Flieger's Splintered Light, do effectively discuss elements of Tolkien's style. Shippey's Author likewise addresses head-on the issues of archaism, diction, and shifting voice... Brian Rosebury also does a commendable job investigating Tolkien's style'; and separately 'Paul Edmund Thomas does an admirable job of looking at Tolkien's style in his investigation of some of Tolkien's narrators.'

claim: Stimpson (1969) charged that Tolkien shuns ordinary diction and wrenches syntax, inventing 'To an eyot he came' as an example.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style'
quote: shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax

verdict.trueWording: shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax
verdict.note: Verbatim including the bracketed [s]: 'Catharine R. Stimpson, a scholar of English, wrote in 1969 that Tolkien not only "shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax". She supported her argument by inventing what she asserted were Tolkienistic sentences such as "To an eyot he came."' The 1969 date and the invented-example framing both match.

claim: Rosebury answers Stimpson item by item, locating the three real uses of 'eyot' and arguing their syntax is unexceptional twentieth-century English that Hemingway could have written.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)

verdict.trueWording: Ernest Hemingway could have written them
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied to check, so this is graded on substance, which the page fully supports. 'Brian Rosebury systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack, showing that Tolkien mostly uses plain modern English. He locates the three places where Tolkien uses "eyot", arguing that "island" could not in these instances be used instead without loss of meaning... All three, Rosebury writes, are unexceptional in 20th century syntax: "Ernest Hemingway could have written them".' Item-by-item reply, three uses, unexceptional 20th-century syntax, and the Hemingway comparison all confirmed.

claim: Rosebury reads the Witch-king passage as making effective use of inversion together with assonance and alliteration to produce a powerfully musical sentence.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Rosebury)
quote: powerfully musical sentence

verdict.trueWording: powerfully musical sentence
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the surrounding analysis matches on every element: Rosebury notes the shift heralded by 'But glad would he have been', 'with effective use of inversion'; then 'The passage ends with a powerfully musical sentence with assonances between "blade", "wield", "dealt" and so on; alliteration with "wield", "wound", "will"'. The passage is indeed the Witch-king one (Merry's blade, 'the sword of the Barrow-Downs').

claim: Turner characterises the base style as paratactic, sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions, with repeated 'and'.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Turner)

verdict.trueWording: sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so graded on substance, which is fully supported. 'Allan Turner... demonstrated with examples that Tolkien's style is both generally simple, using parataxis – sentences without subordinate clauses or causal conjunctions – and varied'. The repeated 'and' is confirmed separately: 'Turner notes that the paratactic style here, with the repeated use of "and" in the manner of the New Testament, is "stylistically marked"'. Note the article pairs 'generally simple' with 'and varied' — the claim's 'base style' framing is fair but drops Turner's second half.

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann define the epic register in LOTR by archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery and poetic description, and count 45 to 50 embedded stories told by 23 narrators.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's prose style' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)
quote: archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery

verdict.trueWording: archaic diction, parataxis with clauses linked with 'and'
verdict.note: Substance fully confirmed; the quotation is not contiguous. The article reads 'The epic style is characterised by archaic diction, parataxis with clauses linked with "and", plentiful imagery, and a richly poetical use of descriptive words' — the claim's quote 'archaic diction, parataxis, plentiful imagery' elides 'with clauses linked with "and"', so it is not word for word. The counts are exact: 'There are some 45 to 50 stories embedded in the text of The Lord of the Rings, supposedly narrated by 23 of the novel's characters', cited to Kullmann and Siepmann 2021, pp. 193–226.

claim: Rosebury traces Tolkien's development from an early sustained archaism modelled on William Morris to the mature intimate paternal storytelling style of LOTR.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'Tolkien's Use of Poetry and Prose' (citing Rosebury)
quote: a sustained archaism

verdict.trueWording: a sustained archaism
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'His prose uses "a sustained archaism" that harked back to William Morris (Rosebury, 95).' The developmental arc matches too: the post attributes it to 'Brian Rosebury, in his chapter "Fiction and Poetry"', tracing 1914–1973, and concludes 'when Tolkien finally achieved the "intimate paternal story-telling" style in his composition of the LOTR, his poetry was no longer conventional pastiche and his prose no longer weighed down by impossibly heavy archaism (Rosebury, 117).'

claim: Le Guin (as summarised) credits the prose with a simple timelessness that avoids both thee/thou archaism and modern slang; Sperling adds that Elrond stays consistently archaic while Aragorn can be wholly colloquial.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog, 'A Hobbit Book: The Simplicity of Style'
quote: simple timelessness

verdict.trueWording: simple timelessness
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'LeGuin calls his language "an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness."' Both avoidances confirmed in the next sentences: 'by not trying to force the reader into a world of "thee" and "thou"' and 'his avoidance of most modern slang keeps his writing timeless.' The Sperling half is also exact — the post is signed '--Micah Sperling' and reads: 'Elrond's syntax and choice of words could be accused of archaism, but it is consistently archaic... Aragorn, on the other hand, can speak in completely colloquial modern English with just a hint of formality in the background.'

claim: Le Guin counted stresses and finds Tolkien's prose runs at the normal narrative ratio of one stress per two to four syllables, rising toward poetry's one-in-two in intense passages.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (The Wave in the Mind, PDF)
quote: one stress every two to four syllables

verdict.trueWording: one stress every two to four syllables
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'Tolkien's prose runs to the normal narrative ratio of one stress every two to four syllables.' The counting is confirmed ('I got interested in the ratio of stresses to syllables in prose, and did some counting'), as is the rise in intense passages: 'In passages of intense action and feeling the ratio may get pretty close to 50 percent, like poetry.' Small precision note: Le Guin's baseline for poetry is 'one syllable out of every two or three', so 'poetry's one-in-two' matches the 50 percent figure rather than her general poetry ratio.

claim: Le Guin insists the prose remains irregular and cannot be scanned, the sole exception being Tom Bombadil, whose speech is verse printed as prose with an infectious beat picked up by Goldberry and Frodo.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: it is irregular, it can't be scanned

verdict.trueWording: except for Tom, it is irregular, it can't be scanned
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the sole-exception framing is explicit: '...but still, except for Tom, it is irregular, it can't be scanned', reinforced by 'If there are other metric passages in the Trilogy, I've missed them.' The verse-printed-as-prose point is confirmed twice: 'once at least in the Trilogy he quietly slips from prose into verse without signalling it typographically' and 'Usually Tom's speech is printed without line breaks, so unwary or careless silent readers may miss the beat until they see it as verse.' The infectious beat too: 'it's an infectious beat; it echoes in Goldberry's speech, and Frodo picks it up.'

claim: Le Guin finds the speech of Elves and noble folk such as Aragorn has a dignified, stately gait without a regular stress-beat, and Théoden only occasionally drops into iambics.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat

verdict.trueWording: dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat
verdict.note: Le Guin PDF p.87 (essay 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'): 'The speech of the elves and noble folk such as Aragorn has a dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat. I suspected King Theoden of iambics, but he only drops into them occasionally, as all measured English speech does.' Both halves of the claim confirmed.

claim: Le Guin describes the narrative in passages of epic action as moving in balanced cadences with a majestic sweep reminiscent of epic poetry while remaining pure prose.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: balanced cadences in passages of epic action

verdict.trueWording: balanced cadences in passages of epic action
verdict.note: Same page: 'The narrative moves in balanced cadences in passages of epic action, with a majestic sweep reminiscent of epic poetry, but it remains pure prose.' Every element of the claim is present.

claim: Le Guin identifies the rhythm shaping the whole narrative as the simplest possible, two beats of stress and release, a walking gait, a trochaic alternation contemporaries found simplistic.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats

verdict.trueWording: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats
verdict.note: p.88: 'The rhythm that shapes and directs his narrative ... is very strong and very simple, as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats. Stress, release... A walking gait'. The 'trochaic'/simplistic element is also confirmed on p.89: 'This "trochaic" alternation of stress and relief...' and 'To readers with such expectations, Tolkien's plodding stress/relief pattern seemed and seems simplistic, primitive.'

claim: Scanning 'Fog on the Barrow-downs', Le Guin found each of a set of polarities (darkness/daylight, resting/traveling, confusion/clarity, menace/ease, imprisonment/freedom, fear/courage) reversed three or four times in the chapter.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal

verdict.trueWording: a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal
verdict.note: Quote verbatim (p.89). All six named polarities are on her list: darkness/daylight, resting/traveling on, confusion of thought/clarity, sense of menace/of ease, imprisonment or a trap/freedom, fear/courage. ONE OVERSTATEMENT: she writes 'Each such reversal or pulsation occurs more than once in the chapter, some three or four times' — 'three or four times' applies to SOME, not to each. Also she names the chapter 'Fog on the Barrow Downs' (no hyphen).

claim: Le Guin notes directionality is important throughout the book, with up and hilltops usually more fortunate than down and valleys.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'

verdict.trueWording: Directionality is extremely important all though the book
verdict.note: p.91: 'Directionality is extremely important all though the book' [sic — 'all though'], and 'Up is usually a bit more fortunate than down, hilltops better than valleys; but the Barrow Downs—hills—are themselves an unlucky place to be.' Both halves confirmed; note she immediately qualifies the up/down rule.

claim: Le Guin holds the chapter is one beat in the book's rhythm and that the structure is both journeylike and architectural, built by repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo and reversal.
source: Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: both journeylike and architectural

verdict.trueWording: The rhythmic structure of narrative is both journeylike and architectural

All three components verbatim.

claim: Zimmer argues much of the prose's power comes from a technically skilled poet: Tom Bombadil's dialogue is in amphibrachs and amphimacers, galloping riders get dactylic and wolves spondaic stress patterns.
source: Wikipedia, 'Poetry in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Zimmer)
quote: written by a poet of high technical skill

verdict.trueWording: written by a poet of high technical skill
verdict.note: Wikipedia 'Metrical variety' section: Zimmer quoted as 'much of the power of Tolkien's "prose" comes from the fact that it's written by a poet of high technical skill, who carried his metrical training into his fiction'; Bombadil's whole dialogue in a metre 'built on amphibrachs and amphimacers'. The horses/wolves line is marked by Zimmer as 'dactyl, dactyl, anapaest, anapaest for the galloping riders; the sudden spondee of the wolves' — the claim drops the two anapaests but is otherwise accurate.

claim: Brauer observes that alliteration crosses from the Rohirrim's verse into the surrounding narrative prose of 'The Ride of the Rohirrim' (e.g. 'Fey he seemed').

verdict.trueWording: makes its way into Tolkien's prose

'Fey he seemed' appears in the quoted prose with the f-alliteration marked.

claim: Thomas, using Booth's scale, finds The Hobbit opens with a very intrusive narrator who recedes as the book darkens, while LOTR's narrator is impartial and self-effacing and early LOTR drafts failed when they tried to return to the intrusive voice.

quote: impartial and self-effacing

verdict.trueWording: impartial and self-effacing
verdict.note: Post body (present in the page HTML): 'the opening of The Hobbit is told by a very intrusive narrator, but as the book gets more serious toward the end, the narrator recedes; and by the start of The Lord of the Rings, the narrator has become impartial and self-effacing'. Booth confirmed in the footnote ('a system from Wayne Booth's The Rhetoric of Fiction ... a scale between unintrusive and intrusive'), and the drafts: 'the initial drafts of LotR, which were unsuccessful attempts to return to the intrusive voice'. Every element checks out.

claim: Litschko describes The Hobbit's narrator as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments on and judges characters, addresses readers directly, and carries a patronising quality suited to a young audience.
source: Litschko, 'The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit' (2006, GRIN preview)
quote: intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges

verdict.trueWording: intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges
verdict.note: GRIN preview (Litschko, 2006, 29 pp.): 'the narrator of The Hobbit is an intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges the characters as well as the unfolding events ... and who addressed his readers in a direct way'. Patronising element confirmed in the excerpt: 'these particular kinds of comments ... still have a somewhat patronising quality to them, as if the narrator was talking to a predominantly young audience'.

claim: Bratman distinguishes four styles in the legendarium texts: Annalistic, Antique, Appendical and Philosophical.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien's Legendarium: Essays on The History of Middle-earth' (citing Bratman)
quote: Annalistic, Antique, Appendical, and Philosophical

verdict.trueWording: "Annalistic, Antique, Appendical, and Philosophical"
verdict.note: Reception section, verbatim: reviewer John S. Ryan notes "Bratman's description of the 4 styles Tolkien used in the Legendarium as 'Annalistic, Antique, Appendical, and Philosophical'". Attribution to Bratman is correct; note the page relays it via Ryan's 2001 review in VII rather than from Bratman's essay directly.

claim: Turner's abstract holds The Silmarillion deliberately avoids conventional storytelling features to create a remote textworld that demands reader effort.
source: Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes' (abstract via OpenAlex)

verdict.trueWording: "deliberate avoidance of stylistic features associated with storytelling makes text-world remote"
verdict.note: The claim carries no quotation to match, so substance only. OpenAlex returns Turner 2022, 'Style and Intertextual Echoes' (doi 10.1002/9781119691457.ch29), whose abstract reads: "The Silmarillion is felt to be a difficult book that requires a special effort from the reader; the deliberate avoidance of stylistic features associated with storytelling makes the text-world appear remote and difficult to approach." Both halves of the claim (deliberate avoidance; remote text-world demanding reader effort) are supported; the source hyphenates 'text-world'.

claim: Shippey's 'impression of depth' arises from casual mentions of an untold background; Drout, Hitotsubashi and Scavera add that apparent contradictions between accounts give readers the impression of a real and complex history.
source: Wikipedia, 'Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: the impression of a real and complex history

verdict.trueWording: "give readers the impression of a real and complex history"
verdict.note: Verbatim: "Apparent contradictions, Drout notes, tend to give readers the impression of a real and complex history", cited to Drout, Hitotsubashi & Scavera 2014, pp. 167-211 — all three names correct. The Shippey half is also supported: he is quoted on depth and on "a coherent, consistent, deeply fascinating world about which he had no time [then] to speak", and factor 2 of the four listed factors is "the apparently casual and incomplete mentions of this background in the text".

claim: Flieger's Interrupted Music presents LOTR as one version of its story embodying references to other versions, with layered narrators, overlapping texts and variants that make the mythology read like a genuine tradition.
source: Wikipedia, 'Interrupted Music'
quote: multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions

verdict.trueWording: "multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions"
verdict.note: Both halves verbatim. Flieger's four levels are quoted directly: "as the story itself; as one version of that story embodying references to other versions; as a historical artifact—the Red Book; [and] as a modern edition of that book" (Flieger 2005, p. 80). The quoted phrase is from reviewer Thomas Fornet-Ponse in VII: "Tolkien depicts his work like a true mythology with different layering, multiple narrators, overlapping texts and variant versions" — i.e. a reviewer characterising Flieger's book, which is how the claim uses it.

claim: The interlaced narrative repeatedly leapfrogs between threads, limits the reader to what one Hobbit sees, and uses synchronising narrative landmarks to keep time shifts legible.
source: Wikipedia, 'Interlacing in The Lord of the Rings'
quote: narrative repeatedly leapfrogs

verdict.trueWording: "the narrative repeatedly leapfrogs"
verdict.note: All three elements verbatim. "[T]he books do not end with the characters synchronised; instead, the narrative repeatedly leapfrogs, so that sometimes one group is ahead in time, sometimes another" (West 1975; Shippey 2005). And: "letting the reader know no more than what one Hobbit sees as he struggles forwards" plus "the use of synchronising 'narrative landmarks', such as the brooch dropped by Pippin and discovered by Aragorn" (Holmes 2014).

claim: Walker holds Tolkien's description sounds vividly detailed while actually giving an open-ended outline that lures readers into filling in the blanks.
source: Tolkien Library interview with Steve Walker
quote: lure us into filling in the blanks

verdict.trueWording: "lure us into filling in the blanks"
verdict.note: Verbatim in Walker's own words in the interview: "tolkien's essential stylistic tactic is to lure us into filling in the blanks". The rest of the claim is also verbatim there: "tolkien's writing, too, sounds vividly detailed, as with his descriptions of hobbits, but he's actually giving us an open-ended outline … that invites us to picture for ourselves what Frodo looks like", and he names "[i]ts invitational quality" as the prose's chief appeal.

claim: Reid's Hallidayan analysis of Theme/Subject in three tonally different excerpts finds shared grammar placing the discourses of mythology and history on a continuum that links LOTR to The Silmarillion.
source: Reid 2009, 'Mythology and History: A Stylistic Analysis of The Lord of the Rings', Style 43.4 (abstract via Crossref)
quote: considerably deeper and richer than critics have realized

verdict.trueWording: "considerably deeper and richer than critics have realized"
verdict.note: Crossref returns Reid, 'Mythology and History: A Stylistic Analysis of The Lord of the Rings', Style 43(4), 2009, doi 10.5325/style.43.4.0517. Abstract verbatim for the quote, and for the rest: "drawing on linguist M. A. K. Halliday's functional grammar, focuses on Theme/Subject and the processes in three excerpts from the novel which are different in subject matter, narrative function, and tone. Despite these differences, a stylistic analysis reveals similarities in the text's grammar that show how the discourses of mythology and history in Middle-earth exist on a complex continuum which unobtrusively connects the novel to The Silmarillion."

claim: Livesey's keyness and collocation analysis tracks the Ring from a central to a peripheral place and from a magical to a burdensome device, registering a tonal fall from faerie to darkness across The Hobbit and LOTR.
source: Livesey 2023, 'The Ring Cycle', Journal of Tolkien Research 18.1 (abstract)
quote: gradual disenchantment of Tolkien's world

verdict.trueWording: "the gradual disenchantment of Tolkien's world"
verdict.note: Verbatim in the abstract of Livesey 2023, 'The Ring Cycle', Journal of Tolkien Research 18(1), Article 4. The mechanism is verbatim too: "techniques of keyness and collocation analysis to trace … a) the Ring's transition from a central to a peripheral place in the Third Age's narrative arc; and b) the Ring's progress from a magical to a burdensome device", across "The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings", with the world "falling from a child-like state of mystery, adventure, and faerie, to one of darkness, hierarchy, and amnesia."

claim: Moorcock's 'Epic Pooh' condemns the predominant tone as the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby meant to soothe and console.

verdict.note: Verbatim and correctly attributed: "The fantasy author Michael Moorcock, in his 1978 essay, 'Epic Pooh', compared Tolkien's work to Winnie-the-Pooh. He asserted, citing the third chapter of The Lord of the Rings, that its 'predominant tone' was 'the prose of the nursery-room … a lullaby; it is meant to soothe and console.'" The word 'predominant tone' in the claim is also the page's quoted wording.

claim: Edmund Wilson (1956) judged prose and verse alike professorially amateurish and the dialogue a story-book language out of Howard Pyle.

claim: Auden's 1954 review credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description.

claim: Rateliff calls Tolkien a very careful stylist who weighed the effect of each word, against detractors such as Medcalf, who read sentences aloud to mock them, and Raffel.

claim: Rosebury (as summarised on Wikipedia) shows the Witch-king passage starting in plain syntax and rising into a higher register when it touches ancient and magical history.

claim: In the same passage Rosebury points to the inversion 'But glad would he have been' and assonance across blade/wield/dealt as deliberate elevation devices.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Rosebury 2003)
quote: But glad would he have been

claim: Tom Simon argues the narrative opens in a jolly Edwardian style, grows more serious as danger rises, and adopts definite formal archaism in the Rohan chapters.

Rising seriousness: 'As the road to Rivendell grows more perilous... the narrative style becomes still more serious and uncompromising.' quote: begins to approximate an older diction

verdict.trueWording: the sentence structure begins to approximate an older diction
verdict.note: Confirmed in context immediately after Aragorn's entrance: 'Once he enters the story, the narrative tone becomes more formal, the prose more cadenced. It is not yet archaic in the strict sense: the words are all familiar to us... But the sentence structure begins to approximate an older diction.' The vocabulary-versus-syntax contrast the claim makes is explicit.

claim: Simon defends archaic inversion by the 'Ask not / Don't ask' test: modernising the word order loses force and rhythm.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: loses force and rhythm

verdict.trueWording: Change Ask not to Don't ask, and the sentence loses force and rhythm
verdict.note: Exact, and the framing matches: Simon cites Kennedy's inaugural ('Ask not what your country can do for you') and adds that changing it to 'Do not ask' is 'even worse'. Used to defend the archaism level found through most of LOTR.

claim: Simon reads the Old Forest chapters as sustained phantasmagoria, Bombadil's speech as loose metre, and the Amon Hen scene as a caesura separating the safer from the perilous half of the story.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)

verdict.trueWording: the effect is one of sustained phantasmagoria
verdict.note: All three parts confirmed. 'In the chapters from "The Old Forest" to "Fog on the Barrow-downs", the effect is one of sustained phantasmagoria'; Bombadil 'speaks in verse - a slightly looser version of the rough metre of his signature song'; and Amon Hen 'serves as a kind of caesura, emphatically separating a comparatively safe and comfortable part of the story from the sharply increased perils and higher tone that come after'.

claim: Reviewing The Children of Húrin, Simon says Tolkien's signature trick is coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary.
source: Tom Simon, The Children of Húrin review (Bondwine, 2007-05-19)

verdict.trueWording: coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary
verdict.note: Exact, in the 2007 Children of Hurin review: 'Tolkien produced many of his best effects by coupling archaic syntax with deliberately ordinary vocabulary.' Context is his discussion of 'haply' as an unusually archaic word for the book, which he treats as the exception to this signature technique.

claim: Simon relays Tolkien's own defence that real archaic English is terser than modern English, illustrated by 'haply' carrying a whole clause of fatality.

page: The Children of Húrin, by J. R. R. Tolkien

verdict.trueWording: Real archaic English is far more terse than modern
verdict.note: Appears verbatim, continuing "; also many of the things said could not be said in our slack and often frivolous idiom." Simon explicitly frames it as Tolkien's own defence: "The best answer is the one he gave to Hugh Brogan". The haply illustration is present too: "That takes twelve words to Tolkien's seven" and "Morwen's almost parenthetical use of haply expresses all the fatality of her decision and the fatalism of her outlook". (My first fixed-width grep falsely reported this absent; the line is short and standalone.)

claim: Simon describes the late Silmarillion prose as a cold and august style that cannot bend to everyday incident, whereas the early Lost Tales were vivid and immediate.

verdict.trueWording: The cold and august style of Tolkien's last years

Like Treebeard, it was 'not very, hm, bendable'." The Lost Tales contrast is also verbatim: that style is "quite different: occasionally twee ... but vivid and immediate". Both halves of the claim hold.

claim: Simon argues The Silmarillion fails to give the reader a point of contact with the legendarium, the anchoring role hobbits perform in The Lord of the Rings.

verdict.trueWording: a point of contact between the legendarium and the modern reader

The hobbit-mediation half is explicit elsewhere in the same post: "it was Hobbits that made it possible for The Lord of the Rings to succeed", and deriving the legends from Bilbo's Translations "would at least have allowed him to introduce the legends in a familiar Hobbit-voice, and given us a firm imaginative vantage-point".

claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) finds truly archaic words like alas, thou, whither are rare; the antique feel comes from words such as deem, moot and wight rather than Old English.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009)

verdict.trueWording: antiquity comes not from Old English but more familiar words
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied with this claim, so verbatim status is not applicable; both halves are supported. Page: "He notes that there are only a few actually archaic words, and that Tolkien uses them only rarely, such as 'alas', 'thou', and 'whither'" and "Walker comments, however, that much of the impression of antiquity comes not from Old English but from more recent, more familiar words such as 'deem', 'moot', and 'wight'". Attributed on-page to Steve Walker, The Power of Tolkien's Prose.

claim: Siepmann shows Tolkien imports words from his own Beowulf translation (valour, valiant, corslet) and stretches them to new uses such as lightning that 'smote' the hills.

feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns

source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)

verdict.trueWording: a black smoke swirled in the air
verdict.note: Verbatim (source prints it after an ellipsis: "… a black smoke swirled in the air."). Surrounding text supports the framing: modern key words "are usually part of the core vocabulary of present-day English" but "Tolkien tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns", smoke "commonly preceded by the indefinite article".

claim: Siepmann notes a modernist trait in Tolkien's abundant descriptive verbs that carry an adverbial manner (clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, loom, peer, plod, stride).

quote: abundant use of descriptive verbs

verdict.trueWording: abundant use of descriptive verbs
verdict.note: Verbatim within "One area in which Tolkien tends to follow modernist tendencies is his abundant use of descriptive verbs", glossed as verbs containing "an additional semantic feature that assumes the function of a manner adverb". All eight verbs cited in the claim (clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, loom, peer, plod, stride) appear in the source's key-verb list.

claim: Siepmann concludes Tolkien's prose deploys several centuries of English at once, putting old words to new uses and vice versa, making him a quiet linguistic postmodernist.
source: Dirk Siepmann, Tolkien as a stylist (CL2017)
quote: he is a linguistic postmodernist

verdict.trueWording: he is a linguistic postmodernist
verdict.note: Verbatim in the conclusion: "far from being 'amateurish', Tolkien's prose effectively employs several centuries' worth of linguistic developments, putting old words to new uses and vice versa. In a much less obvious sense than in the case of James Joyce or Virginia Woolf, he is a linguistic postmodernist." The claim's "quiet" fairly renders "In a much less obvious sense".

claim: Gordon relays Tolkien's point that a king who spoke in modern fashion would not have had those thoughts, so speech register encodes character and culture.

verdict.trueWording: would not have had those thoughts
verdict.note: Verbatim: "But, Tolkien states, a King who spoke in that modern fashion would not have had those thoughts!" followed by "There is an incongruity between modern English and Theoden's way of thinking", supporting the register-encodes-character reading. Correctly framed as Gordon relaying Tolkien.

claim: Ostadan, applying Le Guin, says Tolkien's elevated dialogue works by simple timelessness, the language of men of character, rather than fumbling with thee, thou and mayhap.

The contrast is also on the page: young fantasy writers "fumbling with 'thee' and 'thou' and overusing words like 'mayhap'". Byline and date confirmed: "September 26th, 2022 by Ostadan". Nuance: the phrase is Le Guin's, quoted by Ostadan, and the thee/thou/mayhap charge is Le Guin's against young fantasy writers generally.

claim: Ostadan shows how modernisms such as 'Okay', 'like' and 'conflicted' dropped at random into otherwise timeless speech break the secondary world, the failure Le Guin's Poughkeepsie test detects.

The surrounding paragraph lists the exact modernisms cited: hobbits saying 'Okay,' and 'It means, like, what we do,' and 'Elves who say "conflicted"'. The break-the-world framing is also explicit: 'The spell has broken, and the art has failed: we are back in Poughkeepsie.'

claim: Le Guin's essay (per Wikipedia) holds that in fantasy every word counts and fantastic creation must reach into the words and grammar themselves, naming Tolkien among the writers who achieve it.

The same sentence names Dunsany, Eddison, Kenneth Morris, Tolkien, Cabell, Walton and Vance as successful examples, so 'naming Tolkien among the writers who achieve it' is correct. 'And every word counts' also appears verbatim in the preceding paragraph, quoted from Le Guin.

claim: Rateliff explains that Tolkien's thou marks familiarity (per Appendix F), so Éowyn's switch signals intimacy, but modern readers hear formality, an effect Tolkien aimed for and missed.
source: John D. Rateliff, Eowyn's Thee and Thou (Sacnoth's Scriptorium, 2019-04-06)

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien is trying for one effect and instead achieving another

Substance confirmed: the post sets out the two usages (dominant formal/remote KJV sense, forgotten intimate sense), says the intimate sense 'add[s] an extra layer to Eowyn's laying bare her feelings', and cites the Appendix F 'On Translation' footnote for the familiar/deferential distinction.

claim: Rateliff quotes Appendix F's note that Pippin used the familiar form to everyone in Minas Tirith, including Denethor, a comic register error Tolkien built in.

The comic reading is supported by the next sentence: 'This may have amused the aged Steward, but it must have astonished his servants.'

claim: Shippey (per Wikipedia) contrasts Aragorn's deceptively modern, easy-going range with Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence, using speech to rank the two men.

verdict.note: 'slightly wooden magniloquence' is exact, inside the fuller Shippey quotation: 'Aragorn's language deceptively modern, even easy-going on occasion, but with greater range than Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence.' The page frames it as Aragorn having greater range and 'joust[ing] verbally' with Boromir while asserting his heirship, which supports the claim's 'rank the two men' gloss, though that phrasing is the claim's own, not the page's.

claim: Shippey reads the Gaffer's proverb-heavy talk, many words and few to the point, as the baseline of ordinary speech against which the other registers are measured.
source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)
quote: many words and few to the point

verdict.trueWording: many words and few to the point
verdict.note: Exact match, of Gaffer Gamgee inside Gandalf's monologue. The baseline reading is directly supported by the next sentence: Gaffer Gamgee 'functions as a kind of base-line of normality - and, concomitantly, of emptiness'.

claim: Shippey observes the Council chapter has twelve speakers plus seven more quoted inside Gandalf's monologue, which fills half the chapter, and succeeds as pure dialogue through register variation.
source: Wikipedia, The Council of Elrond (citing Shippey 2005)

verdict.trueWording: twelve of them present, and another seven quoted in Gandalf's speech
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so verbatim status is not assessable; every element checks out. Page: 'twelve of them present in the meeting, and another seven quoted in the longest speech, Gandalf's, which, Shippey notes, takes up half the chapter'; 'in it nothing happens: it consists entirely of people talking'; and the success is attributed to Tolkien's 'unusual ability to suggest cultural variation by differences in mode of speech'.

claim: Meyer, following Shippey, finds Gandalf's speech only subtly archaized, mixing 'nigh' and 'mattered little' with modern idioms like 'for one thing'.
source: Marguerite Meyer, Self-Stylin': Gandalf the Grey (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)

verdict.trueWording: a style that is only subtly archaized
verdict.note: Exact match; post signed '--Marguerite Meyer'. The word pairing is exact too: 'Phrases like "nigh," "learned also," and "mattered little" are clearly archaic and rather formal, but those like "for one thing" and "already guessed" sound much more modern.'

claim: Meyer argues Gandalf is marked by versatility, moving from 'Ass! Fool!' to 'Thrice worthy and beloved' and reproducing seven other speakers' voices.
source: Marguerite Meyer, Tolkien: Medieval and Modern (2014-04-18)

verdict.trueWording: versatility and by the ability to hear and replicate other styles

'Ass! Fool! Thrice worthy and beloved Barliman!' is quoted on the page, and the seven figure is supported: Gandalf's speech 'takes up close on half the total, contains direct quotation from seven more'.

claim: Jaffe argues range of register marks adaptability: Aragorn moves between high and common styles, Elrond stays consistently archaic and formal, and Boromir has no range downward.
source: David Jaffe, The Style of the Elf-Friend (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2014-04-18)
quote: consistently archaic and formal

verdict.trueWording: whose style is consistently archaic and formal (Shippey 70)
verdict.note: Exact match; post signed '--David Jaffe'. Aragorn's range is confirmed ('easy fluctuation between Aragorn's high and dignified style ... and Strider's low, common style'), and 'no range downward' is precisely the page's point about Boromir: 'relatively Elrondian...' but '...shows no sign of knowing anyone of Butterbur's social status'.

claim: The same post describes the mature style as flexible, clear and simple, arrived at after early prose weighed down by sustained Morris-style archaism.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern (2014-04-18)

verdict.trueWording: His style (flexible, clear, simple) feels so effortless
verdict.note: Exact match, as a parenthetical in the opening paragraph. The contrast is supported: the early prose 'uses "a sustained archaism" that harked back to William Morris (Rosebury, 95)', and the mature prose is 'no longer weighed down by impossibly heavy archaism'.

claim: The 2020 post shows Bilbo's 'Hullo!' chosen over 'hail', subject-dropped fragments like 'Feel ready for the great council?' marking informality, and Frodo's 'should like' marking moderate formality.
source: Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, Hobbits at the Council of Elrond (2020-04-22)
quote: Feel ready for the great council?
page: Hobbits at the Council of Elrond

verdict.trueWording: Feel ready for the great council?
verdict.note: Exact match, both in the block-quoted passage and in the analysis. All three sub-points hold: 'If archaism in speech were desired, another greeting, such as "hail" or "greetings", would be used'; 'It is a sentence fragment, omitting the implied "do you" to start the question'; and Frodo's 'should like' 'displays a slight sense of formality that contrasts with Bilbo's casual and colloquial speech'.

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann (per Wikipedia) tabulate Aragorn as archaic and literary, Sam as colloquial, rustic, working class, Gandalf as plain and flexible, Pippin asking questions and Merry making direct statements.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021)

verdict.trueWording: Sam | Colloquial, rustic, working class

Other rows confirm the rest: Aragorn 'Archaic, literary' (and 'archaic and literary' in the body text), Gandalf 'Plain, flexible', Merry 'Direct statements', Pippin 'Questions, exclamations' -- the body text adding 'Merry makes direct statements, while Pippin characteristically asks questions'.

claim: Vaninskaya (per Wikipedia) reads orc speech as twentieth-century soldier and functionary language, including the clipped telegraphese of 'Nazgûl uneasy. Spies feared on Stairs.'
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Vaninskaya 2020)

verdict.trueWording: the clipped language of army dispatches

Spies feared on Stairs." and supports the wider reading - Tolkien gives the Orcs "the speech of the twentieth century, whether as soldiers, functionaries in party or government".

claim: Rosebury calls Gollum's voice Tolkien's most memorable success: obsessive repetition, undeveloped syntax and unstable grammatical person suggesting mental illness.
source: Wikipedia, Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings (citing Rosebury 2003)

page: Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings

verdict.trueWording: "obsessive repetition", "undeveloped syntax and unstable sense of grammatical person"
verdict.note: Substance fully supported but the quotation is not word-for-word: the page has two separate quoted fragments, and reads "unstable sense of grammatical person" (the claim drops "sense of"). Page adds "sufficient to imply dissociative mental illness"; "most memorable success" is Rosebury on Tolkien's portrayal of Gollum, with an "extraordinary idiolect".

claim: Milom's corpus study finds Gollum uses self-referent 'we/us' with non-standard verbs ('we doesn't') and sibilant reduplication mostly on plurals, while Sméagol keeps standard 'I' and grammar the closer he is to redemption.

verdict.note: Exact. Every element checks out: "With self-referent “we” subject pronoun" is listed under Non-Standard Conjugations, the example "we doesn't answer" appears, Gollum is "the more likely speaker to reduplicate sibilants", and "the closer Smeagol is to redemption and rehabilitation, the closer he adheres to standard language rules" (page says "correctly uses personal pronouns" rather than naming "I"). claim: Shippey holds that the simple modern hobbit register mediates between the modern reader and the heroic, archaic registers of Elves, Dwarves and Rohirrim.

claim: Alaric Hall's lecture notes the Rohirrim speak the Old English dialect of Tolkien's own home region and that their verse alliterates on the stressed syllables in the Beowulf manner.

claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) reads the ubi sunt theme as producing an elegiac tone and a sense of deep time and history behind what can be seen.

claim: Le Guin (as quoted by Nepveu) describes the whole narrative as a two-beat pattern of stress and release, inbreath and outbreath, walked at a human gait.

One, two, left, right, on foot, all the way."

claim: Le Guin grounds the book's rhythm in the irreducible simplicity of the trochaic beat and builds from it patterns of reversal (darkness/daylight, trap/freedom) in 'Fog on the Barrow-downs'.

claim: Le Guin lists the devices by which the moral and physical world is built: repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo and reversal.

claim: Le Guin (quoted by Fisher) says Tolkien's prose flows clearly and follows the breath, with punctuation exactly where a reader needs to pause, so it must be read aloud.

claim: McIntosh documents parataxis, short simple sentences joined by 'and', in the Ride of the Rohirrim and the Pelennor Fields, producing breathless excitement (citing Garth).

claim: Turner (per Wikipedia) shows the Pelennor 'and' chains in New Testament manner are stylistically marked, signalling an exalted register despite few archaic words.

verdict.trueWording: stylistically marked

Citation resolves to Turner 2020, pp. 389-403.

claim: Shippey's term 'loose semantic fit' names Tolkien's deliberate use of conjunctions without explicit logical connection, evoking biblical narrative.

verdict.trueWording: loose semantic fit

claim: Mahon reads the Pelennor account as tinged with the elegiac, losses shadowing victory so the reader mourns while rejoicing.

The mourn-while-rejoicing half is also explicit: "Mahon comments that the reader mourns even while rejoicing, in his view 'the essence of great fantasy'." Reference is Mahon, CEA Critic 40(2), January 1978, 33-36.

claim: Walker finds Treebeard's lament obviously poetic in rhythm, and Forest-Hill and Dettmann find Tom Bombadil's speech essentially all in poetic metre.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009; Forest-Hill 2015; Dettmann 2014)
quote: essentially all in poetic metre

verdict.trueWording: essentially all in a poetic metre
verdict.note: Substance holds; the quotation is one word off. Page: "Tom Bombadil's speech, too, is essentially all in a poetic metre" — the claim's quote drops the article "a". Citation metadata on that sentence resolves to Forest-Hill 2015 (pp. 91-107), Dettmann 2014 (pp. 207-209) and Le Guin 2001, confirming the named scholars. Treebeard is Walker 2009 (pp. 140-141): the lament "in its rhythmic sensitivity... is obviously poetic".

claim: Drout criticises the fox passage in Fellowship as a failure of tone that drags the book back toward the intrusive Hobbit narrator, contrasting the successful 'if logs can be said to be contented'.
source: Michael Drout, How to critique Tolkien's prose style (Wormtalk, 2007-04-12)
quote: failure of tone
page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

verdict.trueWording: a failure of tone
verdict.note: Verbatim: "I think this is a failure of tone (moving us back towards the intrusive narrator of The Hobbit) and jarring to the readers", about the fox's thoughts in Fellowship ch. 3. The contrast is on the page too: "'Sam was content, if logs can be said to be contented' works much better as narrative lightening without jarring the reader".

claim: Drout estimates more than half the novel is landscape description and asks whether the same effect could be won with fewer words.
source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
quote: more than 50% of the novel
page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

verdict.trueWording: more than 50% of the novel
verdict.note: Verbatim inside "Without doing tedious tabulation, I would venture to argue that something more than 50% of the novel is devoted to landscape description." The second half is explicit: "I wonder if Tolkien could have been just as effective with fewer words." Note Drout hedges heavily ("without doing tedious tabulation... I would venture"), so "estimates" is the right verb, as the claim has it.

claim: Drout flags 'thrawn trees' as merely ornamental archaism with no descriptive job, while allowing 'grey falling curtains' because repetition layers it into an image.
source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
quote: merely an ornamental archaism
page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

verdict.trueWording: "thrawn" seems to me merely an ornamental archaism
verdict.note: Wormtalk (HTTP 200) carries the quote word for word, and both halves of the claim. Drout declines to credit 'thrawn' with 'an important technical description the way that eyot, laving, louver, dwimmerlaik, etc., do'; of 'grey falling curtains' he writes he is 'a little hesitant' to call it a cliche 'because the recurrent image of the rain as a curtain is significant elsewhere' and gives 'the kind of layering through repetition which creates the "myth" feel of the book.'

claim: Drout defends 'pinnacles or pillars of stone' as a calculated moment of reader confusion matching Frodo's uncertainty whether the forms are natural or carved.
source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk (2007-04-12)
page: How to critique Tolkien's prose style

verdict.trueWording: a moment of confusion in the reader's mind (as in Frodo's)
verdict.note: No quote was supplied, and the page supports the substance in its own words: Tolkien aims 'to produce a moment of confusion in the reader's mind (as there is in Frodo's) when it is not clear if the giant, pillar-shaped things are really carved by men or are natural formations (pinnacles).' Note the framing: in the body this is one of Drout's 'two critiques' ('I also question "pinnacles or pillars of stone"') with a concession following; but the bracketed update at the head of the post does defend it — 'I am coming around to the idea that "pinnacles or pillars" is actually effective rather than flabby.' So 'defends' holds on the update, not on the original body.

claim: Mambrol describes The Hobbit's narrator as intrusive and avuncular, addressing children with rhetorical questions, a style Tolkien later called bad.
source: Nasrullah Mambrol, Analysis of Tolkien's The Hobbit (Literariness, 2021-02-18)
quote: a bad style, as if one were talking to children

verdict.trueWording: a bad style, as if one were talking to children
verdict.note: Literariness quotes Tolkien's 1967 interview verbatim ('There's nothing my children loathed more', qtd. in Annotated Hobbit 76). The rest is on the page too: 'the narrator of The Hobbit is an intrusive voice', 'The narrator's tone, however, is avuncular', 'very much like an older adult telling a story to small children', with the rhetorical-question example 'And what would you do, if an uninvited dwarf came and hung his things up in your hall...'. The page never uses the word 'rhetorical', but supplies the questions.

claim: Litschko classifies The Hobbit's voice as an intrusive authorial narrator who comments, judges and guides, with a patronising quality and a shift of voice in the final chapters.
source: Nadja Litschko, The Voice of the Narrator in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit (GRIN excerpt)
quote: a somewhat patronising quality
page: The Voice of the Narrator in The Hobbit

verdict.trueWording: still have a somewhat patronising quality
verdict.note: GRIN excerpt for Litschko's 2006 term paper carries the quote verbatim. Every other element is present: 'an intrusive authorial narrator who frequently comments on and judges the characters as well as the unfolding events'; 'how they function to guide the reader'; 'theories of Franz K. Stanzel and Wayne C. Booth'; and section 2.4 'Changes in the Narrative Voice' on 'shifts in narrative tone and structure within the final chapters', written after a three-year break.

claim: Kirk (per Rogers) argues the fairy-tale 'Hobbit style' and the later shifts of narration are deliberate attempts to set the mood of each part of the tale.
source: Dylan Rogers, I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish (2010-03-29, on Kirk 1971)
quote: deliberate attempts to set the mood
page: I Would Rather Have Written in Elvish

verdict.trueWording: deliberate attempts to set the mood for different parts of the story
verdict.note: Rogers' post carries the quote word for word, and the framing matches: 'Kirk makes the enlightening point that this "Hobbit style" was deliberate and crucial to Tolkien's world creation. "Hobbit style" refers to the fairy-tale-esque quality with which Tolkien narrates the Hobbit-focused areas of the story.' The mood sentence is about 'these stylistic changes that throw many critics off'.

claim: Tolkien's Letter 247 (quoted on Wikipedia) locates the book's attraction in glimpses of a large history in the background, like a distant unvisited island.
source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings (citing Tolkien Letter 247)
quote: glimpses of a large history in the background
page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings

verdict.trueWording: glimpses of a large history in the background
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the letter number checks out: the ref is named 'Letter 247' in the page markup and resolves to 'Carpenter 2023, Letter #247 to Colonel Worskett, 20 September 1963'. Full sentence: 'Part of the attraction of the L.R. is, I think, due to the glimpses of a large history in the background: an attraction like that of viewing far off an unvisited island, or seeing the towers of a distant city gleaming in a sunlit mist.'

claim: Walker says Tolkien's description sounds vividly detailed but is an open-ended outline that invites readers to fill in the blanks, training wheels for the imagination.
source: Interview with Steven C. Walker (Tolkien Library, 2009-07-22)
quote: training wheels for our imagination

verdict.trueWording: tolkien's style is training wheels for our imagination
verdict.note: Walker interview carries the quote verbatim, along with the rest of the claim: 'tolkien's essential stylistic tactic is to lure us into filling in the blanks'; 'tolkien's writing, too, sounds vividly detailed ... but he's actually giving us an open-ended outline ... that invites us to picture for ourselves what Frodo looks like.' The word 'invitational' also appears earlier ('Its invitational quality').

claim: Walker (per Wikipedia) finds the prose strikingly invitational, relying on suggestion and semantic ambiguities that widen potential meaning.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Walker 2009)
quote: semantic ambiguities tending to widen potential meaning

verdict.trueWording: semantic ambiguities tending to widen potential meaning
verdict.note: Verbatim inside a block quotation the page closes with the attribution 'Steve Walker, The Power of Tolkien's Prose, 2009 [22]', introduced as 'Walker comments that Tolkien uses language to expand his readers' imaginations'. 'Strikingly invitational' is also verbatim earlier: 'Tolkien's writing is "strikingly invitational", relying on suggestion to elicit a vivid and individual response from each reader.'

claim: Auden's 1954 review credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and an exact eye for description, judged by a realism stricter than Malory's age.
source: W. H. Auden, The Hero Is a Hobbit (1954; Eighth Day Institute reprint)
quote: amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description

verdict.trueWording: an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description
verdict.note: Verbatim on the Eighth Day Institute reprint of 'The Hero Is a Hobbit: A Review of The Fellowship of the Ring', footnoted as originally in The New York Times Book Review, 31 October 1954 — matching the claim's date. The Malory comparison is in the immediately preceding sentence: 'the standard of realism demanded today is much stricter than in the time, say, of Malory.'

claim: Tolkien's 1966 letter to Gene Wolfe, reprinted in Wolfe's essay, says he adopted 'warg' because it had a good sound for the meaning and derived 'orc' from Anglo-Saxon.
source: Gene Wolfe, The Best Introduction to the Mountains (2001; scifiwright.com reprint)
quote: had a good sound for the meaning
page: The Best Introduction to the Mountains

verdict.trueWording: "which had a good sound for the meaning"
verdict.note: Wolfe's reprint of Tolkien's letter, dated on the page "7th November 1966", reads: "Warg is simple. It is an old word for wolf … I adopted the word, which had a good sound for the meaning, as a name for this particular brand of demonic wolf". The orc half is also verbatim: "Orc I derived from Anglo-Saxon, a word meaning demon". Both elements of the claim confirmed on the cited page.

claim: Edmund Wilson's 1956 attack calls the prose storybook language out of Howard Pyle, with stereotyped characters and Sam talking lower-class and respectful.
source: Edmund Wilson, Oo, Those Awful Orcs (1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
quote: Story-book language that might have come out of Howard Pyle

verdict.trueWording: "a story-book language that might have come out of Howard Pyle"
verdict.note: Verbatim apart from the claim capitalising the sentence-initial S of a mid-sentence fragment; page hyphenates "story-book" (the claim's prose spells it "storybook", the quote field does not). Both further elements verbatim in the same paragraph: "such characterizations as Dr. Tolkien is able to contrive are perfectly stereotyped" and "Samwise, his dog-like servant, who talks lower-class and respectful".

claim: Wilson finds the terrors feeble and faceless, lacking concrete reality, and the episodes without development.
source: Edmund Wilson, Oo, Those Awful Orcs (1956; Epistle of Dude reprint)
quote: feeble and rather faceless

verdict.trueWording: "they are feeble and rather faceless"
verdict.note: Verbatim: "But these bugaboos are not magnetic; they are feeble and rather faceless; one does not feel they make any real threat." The other two elements are verbatim too: "What one misses in all these terrors is any trace of concrete reality" and "There is never much development in the episodes; you simply go on getting more of the same."

claim: Moorcock's Epic Pooh calls high-fantasy prose the prose of the nursery-room, a lullaby and mouth-music enjoyed for its lack of tension.
source: Michael Moorcock, Epic Pooh (1978; Arena 2 reprint PDF)
quote: the prose of the nursery-room

verdict.trueWording: "the prose of the nursery-room. It is a lullaby"
verdict.note: Verbatim in the Arena Two reprint PDF (14 pages, pypdf extraction): "The sort of prose most often identified with 'high' fantasy is the prose of the nursery-room. It is a lullaby; it is meant to soothe and console. It is mouth-music. It is frequently enjoyed not for its tensions but for its lack or tensions." All three elements (nursery-room, lullaby, mouth-music, lack of tension) confirmed; "lack or tensions" is a typo/OCR artefact for "lack of tensions" in this reprint.

claim: Moorcock says the trilogy has many confused moments where the tension flags completely, yet concedes that at his best Tolkien writes better prose than his Oxford contemporaries.
source: Michael Moorcock, Epic Pooh (1978; Arena 2 reprint PDF)
quote: produce prose much better than that of his Oxford contemporaries

verdict.trueWording: "produce prose much better than that of his Oxford contemporaries"
verdict.note: Verbatim, and the concession structure is intact: "…which is doubtless why his trilogy has so many confused moments when the tension flags completely. But he could, at his best, produce prose much better than that of his Oxford contemporaries who perhaps lacked his profound respect for middle-English poetry." Both halves of the claim sit in one sentence pair on page 12 of the reprint.

claim: Wikipedia records Stimpson (1969) accusing Tolkien of wrenching syntax and shunning ordinary diction and Raffel (1968) rejecting the book partly on stylistic grounds.
source: Wikipedia, Tolkien's prose style (citing Stimpson 1969; Raffel 1968)

verdict.trueWording: "shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax"
verdict.note: No quote was supplied with this claim, so VERIFIED_VERBATIM cannot apply, but the claim's own wording tracks the page almost exactly. Page: "Catharine R. Stimpson, a scholar of English, wrote in 1969 that Tolkien not only 'shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax'" (cited Stimpson 1969, p. 29), and "was rejected by literary figures such as Burton Raffel, partly on stylistic grounds" (cited Raffel 1968, pp. 218–246). Both dates and both attributions correct.

claim: La Porte's writing lesson shows Saruman's persuasion working through register: a gentle question, the tone of a kindly heart aggrieved, calling Théoden 'friend', each line building tension.
source: Chris La Porte, Writing Compelling Dialogue and the Voice of Saruman (Porte Port, 2020-06-23)
quote: of a kindly heart aggrieved

verdict.trueWording: "tone was that of a kindly heart aggrieved by injuries undeserved"
verdict.note: Verbatim. Every element checks out on the page: Saruman "said now with gentle question"; "Calling Theoden a friend … is a ploy to come off as kind"; and the section heading "Dialogue builds tension one sentence, or word, at a time". Byline and date on the page are "Chris La Porte June 23, 2020", matching the attribution.

claim: The Return to Moria studio set as its first writing rule to use only Tolkien's actual words and avoid secondary interpretations, with Salo supplying Khuzdul dialogue.
source: Return to Moria studio blog, Creating an Authentic Tolkien Journey (2024-07-03)
quote: Only use Professor Tolkien's actual words.
page: Blog: Creating an Authentic Tolkien Journey

verdict.trueWording: "Only use Professor Tolkien's actual words. Avoid secondary interpretations."
verdict.note: Verbatim, and it is genuinely FIRST in the studio's list of "a few key values" (the other two: honour the spirit of Middle-earth as described by text, influences and letters; reinforce and never undercut the stakes of the published works). Salo element confirmed: "We turned to famed linguist David Salo … For Return to Moria he invented an entire lexicon and grammar for Khuzdul. He also translated much of the game's spoken dialogue."

claim: Tauber's tokenisation gives The Hobbit about 95,137 tokens and 11,532 types, with just under half the types plain letter sequences and 291 hyphenated forms.
source: James Tauber, Tokenizing the Hobbit (Digital Tolkien Project, 2021-03-14)
quote: 95,137 tokens

verdict.trueWording: "we get 95,137 tokens" … "come in 11,532 different types"
verdict.note: All four figures verbatim: "If we do that, we get 95,137 tokens in The Hobbit"; "The 95,137 tokens come in 11,532 different types. Just under half (5,576) of those types consist of just a sequence of letters … Another 291 types are hyphenated words like hobbit-hole or good-bye." Worth carrying forward: the post's own conclusion offers 95,137 / 95,390 / 95,643 depending on em-dash handling, so the claim's hedge "about 95,137" is the right register — it is the whitespace-split figure, not a settled one.

claim: Livesey's keyness and collocation study tracks the Ring's lexical field moving from magical to burdensome between The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
source: Michael Livesey, The Ring Cycle (Journal of Tolkien Research 18.1, 2023)
quote: from a magical to a burdensome device

verdict.trueWording: "the Ring's progress from a magical to a burdensome device"
verdict.note: Verbatim in the abstract on the article's landing page, along with the method: "It uses techniques of keyness and collocation analysis to trace transformations…", "via the evolving lexical fields within which Tolkien operationalised it", and the corpus scope "across The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings". Citation metadata on the page matches: Livesey, Journal of Tolkien Research Vol. 18, Iss. 1, Article 4 (2023). Verified from the abstract only — the article PDF itself was not opened.

claim: Tolkien argues a king who spoke in modern idiom would not think the thoughts he expresses, so modernising the speech would create a disunion of word and meaning.
source: Tolkien, Letter 171, quoted on LessWrong
quote: an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning

verdict.trueWording: "an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning"
verdict.note: Exact string present on LessWrong. Immediately followed by "For a King who spoke in a modern style would not really think in such terms at all", which verbatim supports the claim's second half (register as cognition). Preceding context confirms the Théoden 'thus shall I sleep better' example. Fully supported, both halves.

claim: Tolkien calls the belief that twentieth-century usage has special validity a delusion and tells his critic to shake off the parochialism of time.
source: Tolkien, Letter 171, quoted in 'Tolkien on Machines, Power, Language, Love, War, and Everything Else'
quote: shake yourself out of this parochialism of time

verdict.trueWording: "Shake yourself out of this parochialism of time!"
verdict.note: Exact string present on the nothinghuman.substack.com page (capital S and trailing exclamation in source; wording otherwise identical). The delusion half is also verbatim-supported: "the extraordinary 20th.C. delusion that its usages per se and simply as 'contemporary' ... have some peculiar validity, above those of all other times". Both elements of the claim carried by the cited URL.

claim: Tolkien insists 'argent' does not simply mean 'silver' and that a fine word should first be heard as sound in its poetic context.
source: Tolkien, Letters, quoted on LessWrong
quote: better to hear 'argent' as a sound only

verdict.trueWording: "to hear 'argent' as a sound only in a poetic context"
verdict.note: The claim's quote as written is NOT a contiguous span. Source reads: "It is better, I think, at any rate to begin with, to hear 'argent' as a sound only in a poetic context, than to think 'it only means silver'." The claim elides 'I think, at any rate to begin with,' between 'better' and 'to hear', so it fails word-for-word. Substance is fully sound, including the 'does not simply mean silver' half: "They think argent 'means' silver. But it does not." Downgraded on contiguity only.

claim: Tolkien says the most moving effect is the sense of a vanished past and stories left untold rather than told.
source: Tolkien, Letters, quoted on LessWrong
quote: the untold stories that are most moving

verdict.trueWording: "it is the untold stories that are most moving"
verdict.note: Exact string present: "A story must be told or there'll be no story, yet it is the untold stories that are most moving." The vanished-past half is also on the page verbatim — "the heart-racking sense of the vanished past (best expressed by Gandalf's words about the Palantir)" — though note the source presents these as two distinct emotions in one passage rather than one fused claim; the claim's conjunction of them is a fair reading of the surrounding text.

claim: Tolkien says he always begins writing from a name, and the name generates the story rather than the reverse.
source: 1964 BBC interview with Denys Gueroult (broadcast 1971), transcript at Tolkien Library
quote: give me a name and it produces a story

verdict.trueWording: "give me a name and it produces a story, not the other way about"
verdict.note: Exact string present at tolkienlibrary.com: "I always in writing start with a name; give me a name and it produces a story, not the other way about normally." Both halves of the claim (always begins from a name; name generates story, not the reverse) are verbatim-supported. Page is headed as the 1964 BBC radio interview transcript; the interviewer is spelled 'D. Gerrolt' there, not Gueroult — a spelling variance across transcripts, not a substantive discrepancy.

claim: Tolkien says that once a story has several peoples on its hands the author must make them different from one another.
source: BBC interview with Denys Gueroult, transcript at uv.es
quote: you've got to make them different

verdict.trueWording: "you've got these people on your hands you've got to make them different"
verdict.note: Exact string present: "I didn't intend it but when you've got these people on your hands you've got to make them different haven't you." Note the context is the interviewer's question about races embodying principles (elves wisdom, dwarves craftsmanship), and Tolkien's answer opens by disclaiming intent — the differentiation is described as a consequence forced on the author, which is what the claim says.

claim: Tolkien says everything he tried to write ahead of time proved no good and that the story grew without control.
source: 1964 BBC interview reading notes
quote: then it grew without control

verdict.trueWording: "Then it grew... then it grew without control"; "all proved to be no good"
verdict.note: Exact string present at themisfortuneteller.com: "Then it grew... then it grew without control". The planning half is also verbatim-supported: "there's no good trying to anticipate, because all the things I've tried to write ahead of time just to direct myself, all proved to be no good when you got there." Caveat on the source's own reliability, not the claim: the page self-labels "NOTE: Incomplete in places" and is a fan transcript of the YouTube audio, so it is a secondary transcription rather than an authoritative text.

feature: laden familiar words for mythic furniture
claim: Tolkien explains he used existing words like Dwarves, Elves and Middle-earth because mythic matter needs words already laden with sense, not everything strange at once.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'Tolkien in Oxford' reconstruction, Tolkien Studies 15
quote: You can't have everything absolutely strange at the outright

verdict.trueWording: "You can't have everything absolutely strange at the outright"
verdict.note: Exact string present in the ORA PDF. The 'laden with sense' half is verbatim too: "it's desirable if you can, necessary if you can, to use words that are already in existence - which have a certain sense and are laden with a certain sense. And therefore I use 'Dwarves', and 'Middle-earth', and 'Elves' and so on." All three named words appear as the claim states. Fully supported.

feature: engineered ugliness of the Black Speech
claim: Tolkien states the Black Speech was designed to be hideous, and ranks sounds as pleasant or ugly by their place of articulation.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'Tolkien in Oxford' reconstruction, Tolkien Studies 15
quote: It's a hideous language, it's meant to be hideous

verdict.trueWording: It's a hideous language, it's meant to be hideous
verdict.note: Present word for word in the Lee reconstruction PDF (p.41), split only by a PDF line break between 'a' and 'hideous'. The claim's second half is also supported: Tolkien says "'l' is on the whole a pleasant sound" and that sounds become less appealing "the further they move back in the throat" (citing 'ach'), plus "those words are ugly... what I find ugly". The page never uses the phrase 'place of articulation', but the pleasant/ugly-by-articulation ranking is explicit.

feature: no narrator asides / no talking down
claim: Tolkien recalls that his children hated narrator asides and anything sounding like address to an audience, which taught him to drop that manner.
source: 1968 BBC 'Tolkien in Oxford' interview transcript, Tolkien Library
quote: They hated asides

verdict.trueWording: They hated asides
verdict.note: Verbatim in the transcript, immediately followed by "They loathed anything that made it sound as if you were talking to a, an actual audience" and his statement that his children "criticised very severely all those things which, owing to bad models, I thought was suitable to put into a children's story" — supporting the 'taught him to drop that manner' half. Minor caveat: the transcript on this page interleaves a BBC presenter (Razia Iqbal) and so reproduces the 1968 audio inside a later broadcast, not a raw 1968 transcript.

claim: Tolkien calls himself a natural niggler fascinated by detail who loves revision.
source: Daphne Castell, 'The Realms of Tolkien', New Worlds, Nov 1966 (Fantastic Metropolis reprint)
quote: I am a natural niggler, fascinated by detail

verdict.trueWording: I am a natural niggler, fascinated by detail
verdict.note: Verbatim. Immediately preceded on the page by "I love [revision]." (bracketed editorial insertion), in the context of revising the next edition of The Lord of the Rings, supporting the 'loves revision' half.

claim: Tolkien says he takes special pride in readers who like his books for the names, and derides SF writers' childish name invention.
source: Daphne Castell, 'The Realms of Tolkien', New Worlds, Nov 1966
quote: praise of those who like my books for my names

verdict.trueWording: praise of those who like my books for my names
verdict.note: Verbatim, in the full sentence "Nothing has given me more pleasure than the praise of those who like my books for my names, whether of English form, or Elvish, or other tongues." The derision half is also on the page: "When they invent names and words, these are apt to take on a quite childish level. The names are absolutely appalling in many cases" — context confirmed as SF writers by the following "But this is not peculiar to sf."

claim: Tolkien concedes The Hobbit caught sillinesses of manner unthinkingly from the children's-book convention.
source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163), Tolkien Estate
quote: sillinesses of manner caught unthinkingly

verdict.trueWording: sillinesses of manner caught unthinkingly
verdict.note: Verbatim, in "it has some of the sillinesses of manner caught unthinkingly from the kind of stuff I had had served to me, as Chaucer may catch a minstrel tag. I deeply regret them." Context is explicitly The Hobbit written 'as a children's story'; 'the kind of stuff I had had served to me' is the page's wording for the children's-book convention.

claim: Tolkien tells Auden that languages and names are for him inseparable from the stories.
source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163)
quote: languages and names are for me inextricable from the stories

verdict.trueWording: languages and names are for me inextricable from the stories
verdict.note: Verbatim on the Tolkien Estate page for Letter 163 to W.H. Auden, in "All this only as background to the stories, though languages and names are for me inextricable from the stories."

feature: aesthetic pleasure in language for its own sake
claim: Tolkien dates his craft to discovering the acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake.
source: Tolkien, letter to W.H. Auden, 7 June 1955 (Letter 163)
quote: acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake

verdict.trueWording: acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake
verdict.note: Verbatim, in "the study of a language out of mere love: I mean for the acute aesthetic pleasure derived from a language for its own sake, not only free from being useful but free even from being the 'vehicle of a literature'." Dated on the page to his school discovery of philology, supporting the 'dates his craft to' framing.

feature: dialectal style differentiation in translation frame

claim: Tolkien states the invention of languages is the foundation and the stories were made to provide a world for the languages.
