feature: narrative formulas imply hobbit or Gondorian authorship
claim: Formulas such as 'before we came to the Shire' imply parts of the Appendices are written by hobbits, while 'as we have learned from the King' points to Gondor and the scribe Findegil, so the annal's first person shifts with its source.
source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018)
quote: as we have learned from the King

verdict.note: Pezzini n.35 verbatim: 'Narrative formulas, for instance, imply that parts of the Appendices are authored by Hobbits... Cf. e.g. LotR Appendix A [Tolkien 2004: 1039] "as they had done for long years before we came to the Shire". Other references instead point to Gondor and to Findegil, the scribe of the king (cf. e.g. ibidem 1050 n. 1 as we have learned from the King).' Quote verbatim. The closing clause 'the annal's first person shifts with its source' is the claimer's gloss, but is directly entailed by the two first-person formulas the footnote contrasts.

claim: Appendix A declares that only selections from its sources, in most places much abridged, are presented, so the annal frames itself as an epitome of fuller documents.
source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), n. 34 quoting Appendix A
quote: in most places much abridged

verdict.note: Pezzini n.34 verbatim: 'LotR Appendix A [Tolkien 2004: 1033] "only selections from them [the sources], in most places much abridged, are here presented".' Quote verbatim; 'epitome of fuller documents' is an entailed gloss on that sentence. Same pagination note as 436 (footnote sits on p.11 of this AAM).

claim: The appendices are full of scribal glosses, later notes and editorial references deliberately matched to the textual history in the Note on the Shire Records, so the frame is realised by formal features rather than asserted.
source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018)
quote: full of scribal glosses, later notes, and editorial references

verdict.note: Pezzini section 1.7, p.11: 'also this latter part is duly harmonised in the text through the use of formal features; the appendixes are indeed full of scribal glosses, later notes, and editorial references that are meant to match the elaborate textual history detailed in the Note on the Shire Records'. Quote verbatim; 'deliberately matched' = 'meant to match'; 'realised by formal features rather than asserted' = 'harmonised in the text through the use of formal features'. Page cite p.11 confirmed against the PDF's own page 11.

claim: Turner describes the prologue and appendices as an elaborate apparatus containing genealogies and ancient annals complete with scribal footnotes and editorial comments, even a discussion 'On Translation'.
source: Wikipedia, 'Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner 2011)

verdict.trueWording: elaborate editorial framing with genealogies, annals, scribal footnotes
verdict.note: Raw wikitext of 'Literary devices in The Lord of the Rings', section 'Pseudotranslation and editorial framing': 'Tolkien then goes much further, constructing an elaborate editorial framing of the entire book, constructing a prologue and multiple appendices... These include genealogies, ancient annals complete with scribal footnotes and editorial comments, even a discussion "On Translation"...' (sfn Turner 2011a pp.15-17, plus Brooke-Rose 1981 and Carpenter). Claim supplies no quote; the page says 'elaborate editorial framing', not 'elaborate apparatus', and the sentence carries three citations with Turner first, so the Turner attribution is by citation rather than by named attribution in the text.

claim: Appendix B primarily contains timelines (lists of years) for the Second, Third and Fourth Ages with only a few brief narrative sections, such as the account of the Wizards.
source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Appendix B'
quote: a few brief narrative sections

verdict.note: tolkiengateway.net is behind a Cloudflare interstitial: plain curl 403, browser-UA curl with Accept/Accept-Language headers 403, and the MediaWiki action=raw route 403. Recovered via the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20260820110221id_/https://tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Appendix_B (200, full article text, page last edited 11 April 2026): 'It primarily contains timelines (lists of years) from the Second, Third, and Fourth Ages and the events of those years. There are also a few brief narrative sections, including a short discussion of the Wizards and how Gandalf received the Ring of Fire from Cirdan.' Quote verbatim; every limb present. Raw archived page, not a summarizer.

claim: The Fourth-Age section of the Tale of Years gives its dates in Shire-reckoning and follows primarily what happened to the hobbits, so the calendar and focus track the compiler's own community.
source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Appendix B'
quote: dates are given in the Shire-reckoning

verdict.note: Same Wayback raw capture, Synopsis sub-section 'Later Events Concerning the Members of the Fellowship of the Ring': 'Chronology of the early Fourth Age (although dates are given in the Shire-reckoning, and primarily follow what happened with the hobbits).' Quote verbatim. The closing gloss about the compiler's community is supported earlier on the same page: 'It was probably at Great Smials that The Tale of Years was put together... with the assistance of material collected by Meriadoc Brandybuck.'

claim: Bowman shows Tolkien blurring the line between story and history in the Appendices, following his stated preference for history, true or feigned.
source: Wikipedia, 'The Tale of Aragorn and Arwen'
quote: history, true or feigned

verdict.trueWording: To Bowman, this blurs the line between story and history
verdict.note: Section is literally headed '"History, true or feigned"'. Body: 'To Bowman, this blurs the line between story and history, something that as she notes Tolkien much preferred, whether "true or feigned"', with the Foreword footnote 'I much prefer history, true or feigned, with its varied applicability...'. The instance analysed (Aragorn naming Arwen Tinuviel, comparing himself with Beren) sits inside Appendix A, so the 'in the Appendices' limb holds.

claim: The Appendices function as a guidebook to the relics of Middle-earth's history and, in Tolkien's own words quoted by Gray, played a very large part in readers' pleasure.
source: Richard Gray, 'The Read Goes Ever On: Appendices' (The Reel Bits)
quote: a guidebook to those relics

verdict.trueWording: the Appendices are something of a guidebook to those relics
verdict.note: Both limbs verbatim on the live page. Gray: 'So by this measure, the Appendices are something of a guidebook to those relics, still within the framing device of the fictional Red Book of Westmarch'. Tolkien (Jan 1961 letter to Allen & Unwin, quoted by Gray): 'the Appendices have played a very large part in reader's pleasure, in turning library readers into purchasers...'. Page hedges with 'something of a'; page writes 'reader's pleasure' (singular possessive).

claim: Siepmann's corpus comparison finds Tolkien uses roughly twice the nineteenth-century key words of his baseline and sets modern words inside nineteenth-century structural patterns so that common English words are rendered strange.
source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
quote: common English words are rendered strange

verdict.trueWording: modern words placed within 19th-century structural patterns; rendered strange
verdict.note: Raw PDF via Wayback (live dc.swosu.edu viewcontent.cgi 403s), Mythlore 41.1 pp. 279-280 (PDF sheet 5). 'Concerning 19th-century terminology, he had a propensity to use about twice the number of key words.' Baseline limb supported: Siepmann compares to 'curated sets of 19th- and 20th-century writings ... 30 and 94 million words', key = 'outstandingly frequent compared to the baseline corpus'. Quote verbatim: 'while the words were modern, they were placed within 19th-century structural patterns of speech, such that common English words are rendered strange to the eye of the reader.' Chapter explicitly Siepmann's.

claim: The fox's thoughts in Fellowship ch. 3 are a failure of tone, an intrusive narrator jarring the reader after ch. 2's seriousness.
source: Michael Drout, Wormtalk, 'How to Critique Tolkien's Prose Style' (2007-04-12)
quote: moving us back towards the intrusive narrator of The Hobbit

verdict.trueWording: a failure of tone ... and jarring to the readers
verdict.note: Live blogspot post reached. Verbatim: 'the narrator's giving us the thoughts (in English) of a fox in Chapter 3 of The Fellowship of the Ring. I think this is a failure of tone (moving us back towards the intrusive narrator of The Hobbit) and jarring to the readers, who, after getting through all of the cute hobbit-business and small jokes of Chapter 1, have all of a sudden entered into a much more serious world in Chapter 2 (The Shadow of the Past).' Every limb present. Drout later concedes 'an irrational dislike' of the fox passage.

claim: 'thrawn' is decorative archaism, whereas eyot, laving, louver and dwimmerlaik are precise technical words with a function.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
quote: merely an ornamental archaism

verdict.trueWording: thrawn seems merely an ornamental archaism; eyot, laving give technical description
verdict.note: Same post, verbatim: 'the "thrawn" trees: everything up to that point is good, but "thrawn" seems to me merely an ornamental archaism. You could make the argument that it provides additional color, but I wouldn't necessarily accept it as giving an important technical description the way that eyot, laving, louver, dwimmerlaik, etc., do in other places.' Both limbs supported; the judgment is hedged as Drout's own ('seems to me'), and commenters dispute it (one notes 'thrawn' is current Scots).

claim: Drout estimates that over half the novel is landscape description and asks whether fewer words would have been as effective.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12

verdict.trueWording: something more than 50% of the novel is devoted to landscape
verdict.note: Raw blogspot HTML fetched and stripped to text. No quote field was supplied, so the verbatim grade is unavailable; the page's own wording is 'Without doing tedious tabulation, I would venture to argue that something more than 50% of the novel is devoted to landscape description', and the second limb is exact: 'I wonder if Tolkien could have been just as effective with fewer words.' Both limbs supported.

claim: A phrase like 'speeding along with little hope of stopping or turning' attaches two ways at once, forcing the reader into small re-parsings of the sentence.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
quote: tiny re-constructions of sentence meaning

verdict.note: 'tiny re-constructions of sentence meaning' appears word for word: 'I think that such tiny re-constructions of sentence meaning are very important in poetry, but others disagree.' The two-way attachment limb is supported by the preceding sentence, which reads the phrase as 'an apo koinu construction: A: "speeding along with little hope" ...; B: "of stopping or turning"'. Note the page spells it 'apo koinu' (the claim's feature label uses 'apo koinou').

claim: The rain-as-grey-curtain image is justified by its recurrence across the book rather than by novelty, producing a mythic feel.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-12
quote: The recurrent image of the rain as a curtain is significant

verdict.note: Exact but for sentence-initial capitalisation: '...because the recurrent image of the rain as a curtain is significant elsewhere in The Lord of the Rings, and here were could have the kind of layering through repetition which creates the "myth" feel of the book.' Recurrence-across-the-book, the mythic feel, and the rather-than-novelty framing (Drout is hesitant to call 'grey falling curtains' a cliche for this reason) are all supported.

claim: Tolkien's rare words (eyot, laving, louver, ninnyhammer, dwimmerlaik) are precise terms that link back through literary reference to earlier works.
source: Drout, Wormtalk, 'Children of Húrin or, Tolkien: The Scholars and the Critics' (2007-04-08)
quote: precise technical terms

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'when Tolkien uses "eyot" or "laving" or "louver," or "ninnyhammer," or "dwimmerlaik," he is using precise technical terms and linking back, through literary reference, to earlier works of literature'. All five words, and both limbs (precise terms; literary reference back to earlier works), are on the page.

claim: The inverted imperative 'Come not between the Nazgûl and his prey' invokes larger literary contexts through traditional referentiality.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-08
quote: makes use of traditional referentiality

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'When Tolkien uses syntactic constructions such as "Come not between the Nazgul and his prey," or "That was a grim meeting," he makes use of traditional referentiality to invoke larger literary contexts.' The page prints 'Nazgul' without the circumflex and calls it a 'syntactic construction' rather than an 'inverted imperative' — the claim's grammatical label, accurate to the phrase but not the page's wording.

claim: The prose is not shallow; the depths it references are simply not the ones the modernist critic knows.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-08
quote: not the depths that the critic knows

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'It is not, then, that Tolken's prose lacks depth, but that the depths which it references are not the depths that the critic knows.' (The page carries the typo 'Tolken's'.) That sentence says 'the critic'; the 'modernist' qualifier is supported elsewhere on the same page, which ties Appleyard and his fellow reviewers to 'most modernistic aesthetic theories... internalized by the reviewers who publish in the Times' and to 'irony, that all-purpose condiment of modernist writers, critics and journalists'.

claim: Reusing annals, key turns of phrase and stock tableaux from Tolkien's own earlier texts makes the writing feel like inherited myth rather than invention.
source: Drout, Wormtalk 2007-04-17
quote: bricolage of previously existing texts

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'Tolkien's work feels like myth rather than invention because it contains the same bricolage of previously existing texts that long-established mythological traditions seem to contain', preceded by 'Nagy shows how Tolkien's incorporation of poetry, annals, key turns of phrase, stock tableaux--from his own previous writings--creates the "mythopoeic" effects of the writing'. Attribution nuance: Drout is reporting and endorsing Gergely Nagy's 'The Great Chain of Reading' ('the most effective explanation'), not advancing it as his own; the claim does not misattribute, but the argument is Nagy's.

claim: The biggest failing in Tolkien criticism is the absence of discussion of his sentence-level writing, word choice and syntax.
source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), p. 123
quote: his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax

verdict.note: PDF fetched as a binary from ORA (67pp, 200) and text-extracted. Verbatim on the page headed 123: 'The biggest failing in Tolkien criticism, however, is its lack of discussion of Tolkien's style, his sentence-level writing, his word choice and syntax.' The cited page 123 is confirmed by the PDF's own running head. Every limb supported.

claim: Shippey's Author of the Century addresses head-on the archaism, diction and shifting voice that characterise The Lord of the Rings.
source: Drout & Wynne, Envoi 9.2 (2000), p. 123
quote: the issues of archaism, diction, and shifting voice

verdict.note: Verbatim on the same page 123: 'Shippey's Author likewise addresses head-on the issues of archaism, diction, and shifting voice that characterize LotR in particular.' (A first whitespace-normalised search missed it only because the PDF extractor joined 'archaism,diction' across a line break with no space; a space-stripped comparison confirms the printed text matches word for word.)

claim: Inside Gandalf's monologue at the Council of Elrond, Gaffer Gamgee's speech ('changes for the worst', 'abide') functions as the base-line of ordinary, semantically empty modern talk.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 107–8
quote: a kind of base-line of normality

verdict.note: Archive.org djvu full text fetched and the <pre> block extracted; OCR line-wraps normalised. Verbatim: 'Within that monologue Gaffer Gamgee functions as a kind of base-line of normality -and, concomitantly, of emptiness.' Both cited phrases are there ('I can't abide changes... least of all changes for the worst'), the emptiness limb is explicit ('As for "abide", as used by Gaffer Gamgee it has almost no semantic content at all'), and the 'modern' limb is carried by 'there is another modern voice in Gandalf's monologue... this is Saruman's' set against 'By contrast with these familiar styles and voices'. The page break '108 THE ROAD TO MIDDLE-EARTH' falls mid-passage, confirming the cited pp. 107-8.

claim: Saruman's habit of balancing phrases so incompatibles are resolved, and his empty words 'deploring', 'ultimate', 'real', mark him by style and lexis as a politician.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 108
quote: Saruman talks like a politician

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'the message is conveyed by style and lexis. Saruman talks like a politician.' The balancing limb and the three empty words are exact: 'No other character in Middle-earth has Saruman's trick of balancing phrases against each other so that incompatibles are resolved, and none comes out with words as empty as "deploring", "ultimate", worst of all, "real".' The passage sits between the page-108 and page-109 running heads, confirming the cited p. 108.

claim: Elrond's Council speech is full of old-fashioned syntactic inversions and words like weregild, esquire, shards, suited to his age.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 109
quote: full of old-fashioned inversions of syntax

verdict.note: Verbatim (OCR breaks 'old- fashioned' across a line): 'Elrond's speech (256-8), as is only suitable for one so old, is full of old-fashioned inversions of syntax and words like "weregild", "esquire", "shards".' All three words and the suited-to-his-age limb are on the page, which falls after the page-109 running head as cited.

claim: Gandalf uses an older vocabulary than usual at the Council, and Isildur's scroll combines ancient words and endings ('glede', 'fadeth', 'loseth') with Gollum-like phrasing.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 109–10
quote: as if to authenticate himself

verdict.note: Verbatim: 'Gandalf himself uses an older vocabulary than usual, as if to authenticate himself' (p. 109). The second limb is on p. 110: 'Gandalf's account of Isildur makes a point through its combination of ancient words and endings ("glede", "fadeth", "loseth", etc.) with sudden recall of the words of Bilbo and Gollum.' Two wording differences, neither changing the substance: Shippey writes 'Gandalf's account of Isildur', not 'Isildur's scroll', and names Bilbo as well as Gollum. Page break markers 110 and 111 bracket the passage, confirming the cited pp. 109-10.

claim: Aragorn's language is deceptively modern and easy-going but wider in range than Boromir's stiff magniloquence, and the contrast carries their rivalry.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 110
quote: Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence

verdict.trueWording: Aragorn's language deceptively modern, even easy-going on occasion, but with greater range than Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence
verdict.note: Shippey p.110 (djvu page marker confirms): 'More subtly Aragorn and Boromir strike sparks off each other through their ways of speech as well as their claims, Aragorn's language deceptively modern, even easy-going on occasion, but with greater range than Boromir's slightly wooden magniloquence.' Quote verbatim; the rivalry limb is carried by 'strike sparks off each other' and by Aragorn 'letting his rival have the last word'.

claim: Dwarf dialogues (Dáin and Sauron's messenger, Elrond and Gimli, Théoden) delight in cool polite surface over passionate interior, so 'not too long' means 'extremely rapidly'.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 110
quote: passionate interior and polite or rational expression

verdict.trueWording: delight in the contrast between passionate interior and polite or rational expression
verdict.note: Shippey p.110, verbatim: 'Their unifying feature is delight in the contrast between passionate interior and polite or rational expression... Thus the messenger's "things will not seem so well" works as violent threat; "not too long" means "extremely rapidly".' All three named dialogues present: Dain and Sauron's messenger, 'Elrond and Gimli swap grim proverbs', 'Theoden King silences Merry'.

claim: Stylistic variation between speakers is Tolkien's thorough and economical way of dramatising ethical debate.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 111
quote: a thorough and economical way of dramatising ethical debate

verdict.trueWording: Language variation gives Tolkien a thorough and economical way of dramatising ethical debate
verdict.note: Shippey p.111, verbatim sentence. The page's subject noun is 'Language variation' rather than 'stylistic variation between speakers', but the whole preceding analysis is of the Council speakers' contrasting styles, so the limb holds.

claim: The whole of The Lord of the Rings works on its larger scale like the Council of Elrond, depending on relished stylistic variation and separate tableaux more than on plot.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, p. 111
quote: the relishing of stylistic variation

verdict.trueWording: the single chapter relies for a great part of its effect on the relishing of stylistic variation
verdict.note: Shippey p.111, verbatim: 'The whole of The Lord of the Rings is on its larger scale like "The Council of Elrond"... just as the single chapter relies for a great part of its effect on the relishing of stylistic variation, so the work as a whole depends very largely on tableaux: separate images of places, peoples, societies...'. The 'more than on plot' limb is supported by the page's own contrast with 'critics or reviewers skimming through for the plot' and tableaux 'there mostly or largely for their own sake'.

claim: Tolkien deliberately emulates Malory's medieval tolerance of semantically loose phrasing ('by stock or by stone', echoing Pearl), which puzzles readers trained on modern exactness.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, pp. 160–1
quote: His emulation of 'loose semantic fit'

verdict.trueWording: His emulation of 'loose semantic fit' does however puzzle many modern readers
verdict.note: Shippey pp.160-1, verbatim. Every limb on the page: Malory 'did not feel this urge towards exactness at all' and 'Malory's insensitivity in this respect (a common thing in medieval writers) had not led necessarily to failure'; "'By stock or by stone' is certainly a deliberate echo of the fourteenth century poem Pearl"; puzzled readers are 'those especially who have been sophisticated by modern literary practice'.

claim: In an exchange containing no archaic word except perhaps 'naught', a strong archaic effect is produced by inverting nouns and adjectives and by adverbs of time such as 'yet' and 'seldom'.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth (chapter on style, 'hovering between styles')
quote: by inversion of nouns and adjectives

verdict.trueWording: a strong archaic effect is produced, by inversion of nouns and adjectives, careful selection of adverbs of time like 'yet' and 'seldom'
verdict.note: Shippey pp.199-200 (Legolas/Gimli exchange at Minas Tirith), verbatim: 'There is no archaic word in the passage, except perhaps "naught". Nevertheless a strong archaic effect is produced, by inversion of nouns and adjectives, careful selection of adverbs of time like "yet" and "seldom", and other less obvious linguistic features.' The source field's 'hovering between styles' is also verbatim in the preceding sentence.

claim: Tolkien could have written the same exchange in modern English, but the discrepancy between modern usage and archaic thought would have sounded bogus, a disunion of word and meaning.
source: Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth
quote: would simply have sounded bogus

verdict.trueWording: The discrepancy between modern usage and archaic thought would simply have sounded bogus, leading to a deep 'disunion of word and meaning'
verdict.note: Shippey p.200, verbatim, and the preceding sentence supplies the first limb: 'It would have been no trouble to him to write the exchange in modern English' (with a modern-English rewrite given).

claim: Manlove condemns the Treebeard/Galadriel farewell for over-worked cadences and a droning monotonous pitch offering only sentimental indulgence or embarrassment.
source: C. N. Manlove, Modern Fantasy (1975), quoted verbatim in Shippey, Road to Middle-earth p. 160 (Google Books confirms 'overworked' on p. 188 of the 2020 edition)
quote: The overworked cadences, the droning, monotonous pitch

verdict.trueWording: The overworked cadences, the droning, monotonous pitch, the sheer sense of hearts charged not with lead but gas, can offer only nervous sentimental indulgence or plain embarrassment to the reader
verdict.note: Shippey p.160 quotes Manlove verbatim; attribution on the page is explicit ('Modern Fantasy by Dr C. N. Manlove, who then goes straight on as usual to spearhead the critical assault and declare:'), and the passage under attack is 'the parting of Treebeard from Celeborn and Galadriel in The Return of the King, p. 259'. The claim's shortened 'sentimental indulgence or embarrassment' drops Manlove's 'nervous' and 'plain' but adds nothing.

claim: Manlove sets Ector's lament in Malory and the Ubi sunt of The Wanderer against Tolkien's farewell as real elegy with something to be elegiac about.
source: Manlove 1975, quoted in Shippey, Road to Middle-earth p. 160
quote: This is real elegy

verdict.trueWording: Compare this with, say, Ector's lament over Arthur in Malory... 'This is real elegy, for it has something to be elegiac about'
verdict.note: Shippey p.160, verbatim: Manlove cites Ector's lament in Malory, the 'Survivor's Lament' in Beowulf, and a well-known Ubi sunt passage from 'The Wanderer', observing 'This is real elegy, for it has something to be elegiac about'. (Shippey adds that Manlove got it wrong: 'As for Ector's lament, it was in fact over Lancelot, not Arthur' - a defect in Manlove, not in this claim.)

claim: Edmund Wilson judged Tolkien's prose and verse to be on the same level of professorial amateurishness.
source: Edmund Wilson 1956, as quoted in Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist' (CL2017)
quote: the same level of professorial amateurishness

verdict.trueWording: prose and verse are on the same level of professorial amateurishness
verdict.note: Siepmann CL2017 PDF, opening sentence, verbatim: 'scathing criticisms to the effect that "prose and verse are on the same level of professorial amateurishness" (Wilson, 1995, p. 59)'. The paper names the critic by initial only ('Wilson, E.'); its reference list gives Wilson, E. (1956), 'Oo, Those Awful Orcs', The Nation, April 14 - i.e. Edmund Wilson's essay - so the forename is a safe expansion. (The paper's own in-text date '1995' does not match its reference list's 1956; that is the paper's inconsistency, not a limb of the claim.)

claim: Anthony Lane observed that Tolkien's high style had hardly been used without irony since Tennyson's Idylls, so reverting to it in the 1950s challenged modernity head-on.
source: Anthony Lane 2001, as quoted in Patrick Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'
quote: Hardly anyone had used it unironically since Tennyson

verdict.trueWording: Hardly anyone had used it unironically since Tennyson's 'Idylls of the King,' and to revert to it with a straight face in the nineteen-fifties was to mount a head-on challenge to modernity
verdict.note: Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction', verbatim, attributed on the page to 'Anthony Lane (2001)' seeing 'the same dynamic in Tolkien's "high" style'; the reference list gives Lane, Anthony. 2001. 'The Hobbit Habit', The New Yorker, December 10.

claim: Curry concedes Tolkien's tone is sometimes sentimental and that the occasional archaic and high style will never suit some readers.
source: Patrick Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction' (Companion ch. 25)
quote: its occasional archaic and 'high' style

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien's tone (not unlike that of Dickens) is sometimes sentimental, and its occasional archaic and 'high' style will never be to some readers' tastes
verdict.note: Curry, verbatim in Curry's own voice, in the passage listing reasons why The Lord of the Rings 'will never have universal appeal'. The quoted fragment matches word for word; the page sets 'high' in curly double quotes where the claim uses single quotes.

claim: Jenny Turner's 2001 LRB essay dismisses Tolkien's prose style in passing without analysis.
source: Jenny Turner 2001, as reported in Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'
quote: dreadful prose style

verdict.trueWording: Turner mentions Tolkien's "dreadful prose style" in passing (cf. Drout 2004)
verdict.note: Curry PDF (raw, pypdf text, p.6): 'Turner mentions Tolkien's "dreadful prose style" in passing (cf. Drout 2004)'. Every limb held: Curry names the 2001 London Review of Books article by its editor Jenny Turner ('Reasons for Liking Tolkien', LRB 23.22, 15 Nov 2001, in the bibliography) and characterises the essay as seeking 'not so much to understand Tolkien or his readers as to place them beyond serious consideration'. 'Without analysis' is the page's 'in passing' (Curry's cf. Drout 2004 points to the analysis Turner does not do).

claim: The reader's impression of archaicity comes partly from over-use of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (CL2017)
quote: three simple lexical causes

verdict.trueWording: impression of archaicity ... partly due to three simple lexical causes
verdict.note: Siepmann CL2017 PDF p.2: 'the impression of archaicity which any reader will experience on reading Lord of the Rings is partly due to three simple lexical causes: the "overuse" of words borrowed from nineteenth-century fiction, the avoidance of words associated with the modern world, and the comparatively dense use of new coinages, unusual grammatical patterns, rare or obsolescent words.' All three causes match the claim exactly.

claim: Keywords shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, thence, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs/adjectives, many obsolete when Tolkien wrote.
source: Siepmann CL2017
quote: so many of the keywords used to describe its settings

verdict.trueWording: four lexical sets; setting keywords 'obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing'

claim: Honegger shows Tolkien's 'thou' carries five functions (poetry, archaism, contempt, emotion, familiarity) that German du/Sie and French tu/vous cannot reproduce.

claim: Nagel argues Krege's modernisation paradoxically creates a new uniformity by narrowing vocabulary range and simplifying archaic constructions.

Nagel ch.1 (p.26): the omissions 'simply narrow down the tone of passage as given in OV ..., creating stylistic levelling not too far removed from what Wolfgang Krege might have meant by OT's "uniform" language' - i.e. the paradox that modernisation reproduces the uniformity Krege charged the old version with. Simplification limb: 'a tendency of simplifying speech patterns'; 'simplified sentence structure'; conclusion cites 'NT's syntactic simplification' and 'NT's over-simplification of OV's lexical structures and stylistic devices'. Thomas Honegger gives possible solutions for this in French and German, but suggests that the small amount of Old English is probably best left untranslated.' Body repeats it: 'the best answer is probably to leave the Old English names and quoted speech untranslated'. Quote exact; every limb exact.

feature: nomenclature not to be translated freely
claim: Tolkien objected as strongly as possible to free translation of his nomenclature, writing the Guide after the Dutch and Swedish versions.

quote: as strongly as is possible

verdict.trueWording: I object as strongly as is possible to the 'translation' of the nomenclature
verdict.note: Same redirect target, raw wikitext. Blockquote from Letters #190 (to Rayner Unwin, 3 July 1956) on Schuchart's Dutch version: 'In principle I object as strongly as is possible to the "translation" of the nomenclature at all (even by a competent person).' The Guide section opens 'Frustrated by his experience with Schuchart's Dutch and Ohlmarks's Swedish translations, Tolkien asked that...', and the lead dates the Guide to 1967, after the Dutch (1956–57) and Swedish (1959–61) versions — so the after-Dutch-and-Swedish limb holds. Note the source objects to translating the nomenclature 'at all', which is if anything stronger than the claim's 'free translation'.

Quote exact; all limbs exact (the judgement is Beregond's, reported by the article).

Turner points out that this cannot be done in French, while in German it remains a common construction and doesn't give an archaic effect.' Quote exact; French, German-unmarked and lost-effect limbs all exact.

Riftedal entries 26 Oct 2003 / 18-19 Jan 2004: "Namnet syns mig helt idealiskt, det later till och med snarlikt det engelska namnet"; the Swedish-reading limb rests on the diary noting "rift" as a Swedish noun of "riva" (ramna, spricka) treated in Helsingborgs Dagblad, not on an explicit "reads as Swedish" sentence. Raw page fetched direct (tolkien.mbor.se, 200).

Claim matches near word-for-word; graded SUBSTANCE only because the claim carries an empty quote field, so there is no quotation to verify verbatim. Raw page fetched direct (fallingletters.ca, 200).

claim: Tom Simon finds Brooks's prose stilted and turgid, alternating between expository lumps and expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue, with names uniformly slipshod.
source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
quote: expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue

verdict.trueWording: "he alternates between expository lumps as such, and expository lumps feebly disguised as dialogue"
verdict.note: Tom Simon (bondwine.com, 22 January 2007, byline present): quote verbatim; "726 mind-numbing and turgid pages"; the summary verdict "in prose, stilted"; and "The names in The Sword of Shannara are uniformly slipshod". Every limb on the page.

claim: Simon cites Shippey's point that readers hungry for heroic fantasy would take any substitute no matter how diluted, and del Rey's targeting of young readers least likely to notice the writing.
source: 1977: Lord of the Rinky-dink (Tom Simon, Bondwine)
quote: take any substitute, no matter how diluted

verdict.trueWording: "they would take any substitute, no matter how diluted"
verdict.note: The sentence is a block quotation Simon explicitly attributes to Shippey's J.R.R. Tolkien: Author of the Century ("he recovers his usual perspicacity, and puts his finger on the secret of Terry Brooks's commercial success"). Del Rey limb: "del Rey bought the book and skilfully marketed it to the demographic group least likely to turn up its nose at the quality of the writing", with the young named as that group ("it was to the young that the Shannara books chiefly appealed"; "Some people simply do not notice the badness of the prose ... most common among young readers").

claim: Dial H For Houston contrasts Tolkien's invented languages with Brooks naming a corner of the map after a direction, and calls the prose flat.
source: Book Review: Terry Brooks' The Sword of Shannara (Dial H For Houston)
quote: the prose is flat

verdict.trueWording: "The book is long, the prose is flat, and the characters are dull and forgettable"
verdict.note: Dial H For Houston, 18 Nov 2014: quote verbatim; the contrast is explicit - "Tolkien plotted out histories, wrote songs, hell, made up entire languages when he created Middle Earth. Brooks, on the other hand ... let's look at the map", then "You can name one corner of the map after a direction. One. Anything more is just lazy."

claim: Attebery said Shannara tries to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions, reducing Tolkien to a bare formula; Jane Yolen saw derivative fantasy sinking into pastel unicorns and coy talking swords.
source: Tolkien's impact on fantasy (Wikipedia)
quote: pastel unicorns, coy talking swords

verdict.trueWording: "to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions" ... "to a bare formula"
verdict.note: Wikipedia raw wikitext: "Attebery wrote that it attempted 'to evoke wonder without engaging the mind or emotions', reducing Tolkien's artistry 'to a bare formula'"; Yolen on Tolkienesque books: "what began in grace and power easily degenerated into a kind of mythic silliness", with "pastel unicorns, coy talking swords, and a paint-by-number medieval setting" - the claim's quote verbatim.

claim: Le Guin characterised Tolkien's prose as quieter English of simple timelessness with sobriety, wit and force, ranging easily from the commonplace to the stately and able to slide into metrical poetry.
source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)
quote: sobriety, wit and force

verdict.trueWording: quieter... simple timelessness... sobriety, wit and force
verdict.note: Blogspot post quotes Le Guin: 'quieter and [with] a less extraordinary English, or rather an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness... It has sobriety, wit and force... It ranges easily from the commonplace to the stately, and can slide into metrical poetry'. Quote 'sobriety, wit and force' verbatim; every limb (timelessness, sobriety/wit/force, commonplace-to-stately range, metrical poetry) on the page.

claim: Tolkien defended Théoden's archaic speech on the ground that modern dialogue would create an insincerity of thought and a disunion of word and meaning, and gave Elrond the most archaisms as the eldest speaker.
source: It's intentional (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2011)
quote: a disunion of word and meaning

verdict.trueWording: an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning
verdict.note: Page: 'Responding to criticism of Theoden's dialogue in "The Golden Hall", Tolkien claims that to utilize a modern style would result in, "an insincerity of thought, a disunion of word and meaning."' and 'Elrond, the oldest of the council has lived since the First Age, and speaks with the most archaisms as a result of this' (attributed there to Shippey's analysis). Both limbs verbatim-supported.

claim: Le Guin faulted Zelazny and Leiber for talking colloquial American English when humour is intended and reverting to old formal usages at earnest moments.
source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
quote: at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages

verdict.trueWording: When humour is intended the characters talk colloquial American English
verdict.note: Murray Ewing page: 'says Leiber and Zelazny could do better ("When humour is intended the characters talk colloquial American English, or even slang, and at earnest moments they revert to old formal usages.")'. Quote verbatim; both limbs and both authors named.

claim: Le Guin's test is to change a passage's names to mundane ones and see whether it still reads as fantasy; Kurtz's Deryni fails as fancy dress.
source: The Language of the Night by Ursula K Le Guin (Murray Ewing)
quote: fancy dress

verdict.trueWording: change the names... see if it still reads as fantasy
verdict.note: Page: 'The test is simple: take any passage, change the names from mock-fantasy ones to mundane ones, and see if it still reads as fantasy. She uses as an example a passage from Katherine Kurtz's Deryni series... it's not fantasy, it's fancy dress.' Quote 'fancy dress' verbatim. Minor nuance recorded, not a limb failure: the 'fancy dress' verdict is the blogger's own phrase about Le Guin's example, and the claim does not attribute it to Le Guin.

claim: Applying Le Guin, TheOneRing.net found The Rings of Power's 'Okay', 'like', 'Nah', 'Yeah' and 'conflicted' expose modern minds, while its over-correction lapses into fortune-cookie 'High Aphorism'.
source: From The Rings of Power to Poughkeepsie (TheOneRing.net, 2022)
quote: High Aphorism

verdict.trueWording: these Elves too frequently lapse into High Aphorism
verdict.note: TheOneRing.net (26 Sep 2022) lists verbatim: hobbits who say 'Okay,' 'It means, like, what we do'; Numenoreans who say 'Nah'; Elves who say 'conflicted'; Dwarves who say 'Yeah'. 'Instead, however, these Elves too frequently lapse into High Aphorism' and 'we get fortune-cookie philosophy'. The modern-mind limb is the article's own argument ('a disunity of language and character. The spell has broken'; a king in modern idiom would not think 'Thus shall I sleep better'), and the over-correction limb is 'Overcompensating for modernism is, of course, an equally dangerous trap.'

claim: Le Guin's essay separates the risky inner lands of Elfland from banal imitation that is the outside world in disguise, and Beagle called it the definitive piece on fantasy.
source: From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (Wikipedia)
quote: the definitive piece on fantasy

verdict.trueWording: genuine, risky Inner Lands... banal imitation... outside world in disguise
verdict.note: Wikipedia: 'she distinguishes "the genuine, risky Inner Lands (Elfland) from the banal imitation which is really the outside world in disguise (Poughkeepsie)"' and 'The novelist Peter S. Beagle called it "the definitive piece on fantasy..."'. Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

claim: Brennan observes writers sticking '-st' on every second-person verb and '-th' on every third-person one, and warns archaic grammar is very easily overused.
source: Archaic Grammar (Marie Brennan, Swan Tower)
quote: very easily overused

verdict.trueWording: stick '-st' on the end of every second-person verb
verdict.note: Swan Tower page (c 2026 Marie Brennan, footer): 'Some writers seem unable to resist the urge to stick "-st" on the end of every second-person verb and "-th" on the end of every third-person one, no matter what it is.' and 'But archaic grammar is something that is very easily overused.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

claim: 'From whence it came' is a common archaism error because 'whence' already contains 'from'.
source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
quote: from whence

verdict.trueWording: whence already incorporates 'from'
verdict.note: Page quotes the Fellowship film line 'cast back into the fiery chasm from whence it came', then: 'this line uses "from" as well as "whence", which isn't really necessary as whence already incorporates "from"... this article suggests that not only is this wrong, but this is an error English speakers have been making for quite a long time.' Quote 'from whence' verbatim; reason limb explicit. Recorded nuance, not a limb failure: the author hedges ('I'd hesitate to proclaim this grammatically incorrect because I'm no expert') and sources the 'error' judgement to a linked article.

claim: Bored of the Rings steps through the prologue, the map and the main text in turn, substituting brand names (Moxie and Pepsi, Serutan) for Tolkien's invented terms.

verdict.note: No quote field supplied, so graded on substance. Wikipedia: 'The parody steps through The Lord of the Rings, in turn mocking the prologue, the map, and the main text. The text combines slapstick humor with deliberately inappropriate use of brand names.' Brand-name limb: 'the carbonated beverages Moxie and Pepsi replace Merry and Pippin' and 'Saruman is satirised as Serutan, a laxative'. Every limb supported almost word for word.

claim: The parody replaces Tolkien's Sindarin hymn with nonsense modern references ('Unicef clearasil') and parodies the Watcher in the Water as a thesaurus-monster.

Sing hey nonny nembutal", mocking the Sindarin hymn A Elbereth Gilthoniel.' and 'In a parody of the Fellowship's encounter with the Watcher in the Water, the chapter includes: "Aiyee!" shouted Legolam. "A Thesaurus!" "Maim!" roared the monster. "Mutilate, mangle, crush. See HARM."' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported.

claim: David Bratman remarked that the parodists wrought better than they knew, since Tolkien's drafts came close to writing the parody version of his own novel before he avoided it.

verdict.note: Wikipedia: 'The Tolkien scholar David Bratman, writing in Mythlore, quotes an extended passage... commenting "Those parodists wrought better than they knew". He explains that Tolkien, in his many drafts, came very close to "inadvertently writing the parody version of his own novel", though in the end he managed to avoid that, in Bratman's view, remarkably completely.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

Claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

Limb 2: 'there are copious inserted poems and songs, after the manner of Tolkien.' All limbs supported.

claim: Pechey Ponderings notes the parody's embedded songs are well-crafted and its foreword disclaims any attempt to fill Tolkien's shoes.

The page says they 'open with the admission' rather than naming a foreword; claim carried no quote string, so substance grade.

Note the quotation sits in the post's comment thread, not the post body.

Every limb supported, but the claim's quote string drops 'they are', so it is not word for word - substance, not verbatim.

claim: The English Student review reads entries from 'Stew' to 'Reek of Wrongness' as exposing a tour of something made just strange enough to fascinate, with Tolkien as the deeply English conservative template.

claim: Brundige reports Sibley and Bakewell use Tolkien's words almost exclusively except for stage directions, and shun flashback and the narrator's voice as much as possible.

verdict.note: Roger Edwards: 'Great care was taken with pronunciation of words and the delivery of dialogue spoken in Elvish and the Black Speech.' and 'The characterisations and dialogue were extremely well realised'. Quote verbatim; the fetched page is the 24 Nov post itself, not a snippet.

claim: Tolkien told Tiller in 1956 that dramatisation results in too great an emphasis on dialogue, mostly with its setting removed.
source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)
quote: too great an emphasis on dialogue

verdict.note: Wikipedia quotes Tolkien to Tiller, November 1956: 'it requires rather the older art of the reading "mime", than the more nearly dramatic, which results in too great an emphasis on dialogue (mostly with its setting removed)'. Quote verbatim; date and addressee both on the page (ref #194 to Terence Tiller, 6 November 1956).

claim: In 1957 Tolkien wrote he would find vulgarisation less painful than the sillification achieved by the BBC.
source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)
quote: sillification

verdict.note: Wikipedia: 'Replying to Rayner Unwin in 1957 ... he wrote: "I think I should find vulgarization less painful than the sillification achieved by the B.B.C."' Quoted word 'sillification' verbatim; year and sense exact (page spells vulgarization with a z).

feature: dialogue preserved as far as possible
claim: Tiller promised Tolkien that the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible, with a narrator linking scenes and cutting preferred to summarising.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: preserved as far as possible

verdict.trueWording: Tiller: 'the dialogue of the original book would be preserved as far as possible'
verdict.note: Lee, p.2: Tiller's 2/2/55 reply carries the quote verbatim; 'A Narrator would be used to link scenes'; 'Cutting would be necessary... but he preferred this to excessive summarising'. Every limb on the raw PDF text.

claim: Tiller admitted that a great deal of the flavour of the work had been lost through telescoping incidents, and Tolkien replied he did not think more could have been done in the time.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: a great deal of the flavour

verdict.trueWording: 'inevitably a great deal of the flavour of your work has been lost'
verdict.note: Raw PDF: Tiller 21/9/55 quote verbatim, then 'Tiller had therefore telescope[d] incidents'; Tolkien 27/9/55: 'I do not think that with the time at your disposal you could have done any better'.

claim: Tolkien rejected the expectation that hobbits should pipe and squeak, asking why tones should rise with fall in stature, and judged the Elves managed excellently, the Council of Elrond masterly, and Bilbo bored.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: Why should tones rise with fall in stature?

verdict.trueWording: 'Why should tones rise with fall in stature?'
verdict.note: Raw PDF: quote verbatim; same sentence carries Hobbits should 'pipe and squeak', Elves 'managed excellently', Council of Elrond 'masterly', Bilbo sounded 'bored'. All five limbs present.

claim: Tolkien liked Glóin's accent but found it heavily laid on, noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively with a uvular back R.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: heavily laid on

verdict.trueWording: 'heavily laid on'; 'dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively... uvular back R'
verdict.note: Raw PDF: 'He liked Gloin's accent but added it was a bit heavily laid on noting dwarves spoke the Common Tongue natively, like Jews, but they had a uvular back R'. Claim omits 'like Jews' but adds nothing unsupported.

claim: A 1955 review held that Tolkien's relaxed, vivid and masculine style with its rich coinages adapted naturally to radio and held attention even when expository.

quote: relaxed, vivid, and masculine style

verdict.trueWording: 'relaxed, vivid, and masculine style with its rich coinages'
verdict.note: Raw PDF: uncatalogued clipping review 'The Meaning of the Ring' 15/11/55 (so 1955); 'adapted naturally to radio'; 'holds the attention even when he is being expository'.

claim: Listeners to the compressed Series Two called it an absolute ruin and a farce whose ignominious compression produced a juvenile adventure story.
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story

verdict.note: Raw PDF: all four phrases in one sentence about Series Two; the claim's quote field 'footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story' is also verbatim in the following Civil Servant listener comment.

claim: The 1979 Mind's Eye version removed much back history and expository narration and, with lines recorded separately, produced curiously stilted exchanges of dialogue and frequent mispronunciations.

verdict.note: Raw page: 'much of the back history, lore and expositionary narration removed'; 'the cast often recorded their lines separately resulting in some curiously stilted exchanges'; 'The pronunciation of many names and places are often incorrect'.

claim: Wikipedia notes the Virginia theatre players of the 1979 adaptation had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places, though the version kept Tom Bombadil.
source: The Lord of the Rings (1979 radio series) (Wikipedia)

verdict.trueWording: 'had difficulty pronouncing the names of characters and places'

claim: The same post holds that Jackson introduces ironic mockery of characters, a mode Tolkien never uses, and cuts nearly all verse that distinguished the peoples.
source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien 'never operates on an ironic level'; 'verse is very rarely present'
verdict.note: Raw page: movies 'take multiple breaks to laugh at characters, mainly Merry, Pippin, or Gimli'; 'Tolkien never poked direct fun at the characters'; poems 'distinguish the different races of Middle Earth' yet verse is very rarely present in Jackson. Claim is paraphrase, not quotation (empty quote field).

claim: Croft's 'Mithril Coats and Tin Ears' argues Jackson and Zimmerman flattened Tolkien's characters, dialogue and plot and showed too much too soon.
source: Tolkien on Film (Wikipedia)
quote: flattened

verdict.trueWording: Croft argues both men 'flatten[ed]' Tolkien's characters, dialogue, and plot
verdict.note: Raw Wikipedia text of the Mithril Coats and Tin Ears row: 'both men' = Jackson and Morton Zimmerman; 'too much too soon' is supported by 'where Tolkien subtly builds tension, Jackson habit[ually] gives away what will happen' and the essay's 'Anticipation'. The page renders the quoted word with a bracketed inflection, 'flatten[ed]'.

claim: Walker finds Tolkien uses few actually archaic words yet achieves a nostalgic, maybe even archaic essence through words like 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' and 'westering'.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)
quote: few actually archaic words

verdict.trueWording: 'only a few actually archaic words'; 'nostalgic, maybe even archaic'
verdict.note: Raw Wikipedia text, Syntax and diction: Walker on 'only a few actually archaic words'; diction 'manages to seem in its essence nostalgic, maybe even archaic'; and antiquity coming from 'deem', 'moot', 'wight' combined with still-current 'darkling' and 'westering'.

claim: Vaninskaya observes the Orcs speak the most modern idiom in the book, the clipped language of army dispatches and bureaucrats.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)
quote: clipped language of army dispatches

verdict.trueWording: "the clipped language of army dispatches" (Vaninskaya, quoted verbatim)
verdict.note: Raw wikitext of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolkien's_prose_style fetched with a browser UA via ?action=raw. Section 'Varied dialogue types for the enemy': 'Anna Vaninskaya writes that the most modern idiom in The Lord of the Rings is used by the Orcs overheard by Frodo and Sam in Mordor. Tolkien gives them the speech of the twentieth century, whether as soldiers, functionaries in party or government, or "minor officials in a murderous bureaucracy".' Two sentences later: 'She writes that Tolkien captures, too, "the clipped language of army dispatches"'. Every limb supported: Vaninskaya as attributor, most-modern-idiom, Orcs, army dispatches, bureaucrats.

claim: The Riders of Rohan receive the fullest archaic treatment, with rescued Old English words such as éored, dwimmerlaik and mearas and actual Old English phrases.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

verdict.trueWording: goes furthest with Riders of Rohan; words 'rescued from total obscurity'
verdict.note: No quotation supplied in the claim, so graded on substance; the page nevertheless carries the claim's distinctive words verbatim. Section 'Incorporating the archaic, even Old English': 'Tolkien goes furthest with the Riders of Rohan, giving them "Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns" ... He gives Rohan speakers words "rescued from total obscurity" like "éored", Old English for "a troop of cavalry", "dwimmerlaik", and "mearas".' The actual-phrases limb: 'Finally, Tolkien has his Riders of Rohan speak a few phrases directly in Old English, as when Éomer shouts "Westu Théoden hál!"'. All three limbs supported.

claim: The Lord of the Rings contains 45-50 embedded stories told by 23 characters; about half the novel is dialogue, poetry or character-narrated tales and 85% of the narrative is from a Hobbit perspective.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

verdict.trueWording: some 45 to 50 stories, 23 characters, about half dialogue, 85% Hobbit
verdict.note: No quotation supplied, so graded on substance; all three figures match exactly. Section 'Narrative quality': 'There are some 45 to 50 stories embedded in the text of The Lord of the Rings, supposedly narrated by 23 of the novel's characters. ... About half of The Lord of the Rings consists of dialogue, poetry, or stories told by a character. The other half is narrative, often from the point of view of one of the characters, and usually – 85% of the time – a Hobbit protagonist.' (Kullmann and Siepmann). The 85% is of the narrative half specifically, which is what the claim says.
